activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: In her 2017 book 'Radical Candor', Kim Scott argues good feedback combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly.
story:
The problem had followed Naomi home from robotics, and now it sat at the dinner table beside her, unnoticed by everyone else. Across the table her brother Theo was telling their parents about his group project, laughing a little as he described how his lab partner had mislabeled an entire data set and nobody had said anything until the grade came back. "We didn't want to make it weird," Theo said, spooning more rice. "So we all just let it ride."

Naomi put down her fork. "That's exactly what happened with us." She told them about Marisol, who had built the drive-train mount off spec twice, and how the whole team had praised her effort in the meeting afterward and said nothing about the spec. Then the mount failed the drop test on Thursday, in front of the judges, and Marisol had stood there red-faced while everyone pretended it was bad luck. "I said it was the plywood," Naomi said. "It wasn't the plywood."

Her mother tilted her head. "So why didn't anyone tell her?"

"Because she's my friend," Naomi said, and heard how thin it sounded the moment she said it. "Because she works harder than anyone and it felt like kicking her."

Theo, who was seventeen minutes older than Naomi and never let her forget it, was quiet for once. He pushed edamame around his plate. Their father launched into one of his garrulous stories about a colleague who had been "brutally honest" at work and made enemies for a decade, a story that circled the airport without landing, and Naomi stopped listening halfway through. She was thinking about Priya, the team captain, who had stayed after the meeting last week and said, quietly, "Somebody has to talk to her before regionals," and then looked at Naomi and left it there.

After dinner she went up to her room and called Priya. "I'll do it," Naomi said. "But I don't know how to say it without it being either nothing or cruel." Priya said she'd been reading something her mom left on the coffee table, a book from 2017 called Radical Candor, and that the whole idea was that good feedback meant caring personally about someone and challenging them directly, both at once, not one or the other. "That's it," Naomi said slowly. "That's the part I kept missing. I thought I had to choose."

She thought about it while she drafted a message and deleted it, then drafted again. Her old instinct, the nice one, would have produced some version of "the mount was so close, you tried so hard," which would instantiate exactly the silence that had already cost them one competition. The other extreme, the one her father's colleague practiced, was just an insult wearing a virtue costume. Somewhere between silence and insult there was a narrow path, and she couldn't quite see it, only feel where it wasn't.

Saturday morning she found Marisol in the shop before anyone else arrived, already sanding the new mount. Naomi's hands were cold. "Can I show you something before you cut that?" She laid the old mount on the bench next to the drawings. "See where the holes are a quarter inch off the spec line? That's what failed Thursday. Not the plywood, like I said. I lied about that, and I'm sorry." Marisol's jaw went tight, and Naomi kept going because stopping now would be its own kind of lie. "I'm telling you because you're the best builder we have and we need you at regionals, and because I should have said something three weeks ago instead of letting you walk into the drop test."

Marisol looked at the holes for a long time. Then she picked up the drawing and held it against the failed mount, and Naomi watched her see it, the small drift she must have measured around without noticing. "Why didn't anyone say anything," Marisol said, not quite a question. "I don't know," Naomi said. "I think we thought we were being kind." Marisol snorted, and marked the drawing with a pencil, twice. "Okay," she said. "Next time tell me the day I do it, not the day it breaks."

They cut the new mount together, both of them checking the spec line out loud before each pass of the saw, an arrangement so obvious in hindsight that Naomi almost laughed. It wasn't fixed, exactly; she could still feel a thin place in the air between them, and she didn't know whether it would close or harden by regionals. But when Marisol clamped the piece down and said "measure it again, and I mean actually say the number this time," Naomi read the dial and said, "Quarter inch on the line," and Marisol nodded once, like it was a kind of thanks.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In Ontario, when a fixed-term lease ends, the tenant does not have to sign a new one; the tenancy continues month to month automatically on the same terms.
story:
The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and paper. Landon took a number from the dispenser, 47, and sat down beside his grandfather, who had already taken off his hat and set it on his knee like a small patient animal. The light above the tellers read 41. On the table in front of them lay two printed leases, one for an apartment on Gladstone Avenue and one for a unit above a laundromat on Weston Road. Landon had spread them out with the pages overlapping, a spreadsheet on his phone weighted on top.

He was here to open a student account, but the appointment was at eleven and it was ten forty, and his grandfather had said, "Might as well use the time," so here they were, using the time. Landon worked a pencil down the margin of the first lease. Rent, nine hundred and fifty. Utilities, hydro not included, water included. He wrote "hydro?" and underlined it twice.

"That one's a year lease," his grandfather said, tapping the Gladstone pages. "The other one's only eight months. Ends in April."

"That's worse, isn't it? Then I have to sign again and they can change things."

His grandfather tilted his hand back and forth, a gesture that meant neither yes nor no. In Ontario, he said, when a fixed-term lease ends, you don't have to sign a new one. The tenancy continues month to month automatically, on the same terms. Landon stopped writing.

"Automatically?"

"Automatically. Same terms. You just keep paying and keep living there."

Landon looked at the eight-month lease with new attention. It was not a trap; it was a door that stayed open. He pulled the phone spreadsheet closer and started a second column beside the first, dividing the leases into what they cost per month and what they cost per month if the month-to-month part went on past the term. The numbers did not transmute into anything simpler. They stayed stubborn and particular.

Number 44 was called. A woman at the counter argued about a hold on a cheque, her voice carrying across the carpet. Landon's grandfather leaned over the second lease, the one above the laundromat, and read aloud in a murmur: "Tenant responsible for own utilities, all." "All" meant hydro, water, and heat, and heat above a laundromat in January was not a small thing, though the rent was sixty dollars less. Landon remembered his mother saying that a cheap apartment with utilities excluded was a peccadillo that could turn into a crisis by February, and he had not known what the word meant then and had looked it up, a small sin, a minor fault. He wrote "heat?? call" in the margin.

"So the eight-month one," he said slowly, "if I don't sign anything new, it just keeps going. Same rent, same everything."

"Same terms," his grandfather said. "That's what I said to Mrs. Okafor, when her landlord kept pushing papers at her. She didn't sign, and nothing happened. Nothing bad, I mean. She's still there."

"So a landlord pushing a new one-year lease isn't pushing something I need."

"You can sign if you want. Some people like the certainty. But you don't have to." His grandfather put his hat back on, then took it off again, a small restless cycle.

Landon added a third row to the spreadsheet: deposit, first and last month's rent, which both leases wanted, which meant the real cost of moving in was not the monthly cost at all. He had twelve thousand saved from two summers at the garden centre and a season of birthday cheques he had never spent, and the numbers in front of him were the first honest accounting of what independence actually charged. It was not a seismic realization, nothing so dramatic; it was arithmetic. But arithmetic, done properly, had its own weight. He underlined the total for the Gladstone apartment, one thousand and forty if hydro ran ninety a month, and the laundromat unit, nine hundred and ninety if heat and water together came in under a hundred and forty, which he did not know, and could not know from a bank chair.

That was the part that stayed uncertain. He could compare the leases line by line, but the utilities were guesses, and the guesses were the difference between them. He wrote both totals, circled neither, and turned the pencil over and over between his fingers.

"Forty-seven," the light said.

He gathered the pages, squaring their edges against the table. At the new-accounts desk a young banker named Priya asked for his student letter and his identification, and slid a form toward him with a pen chained to a clipboard. While she keyed his information into the computer, he laid the leases out again on the counter, because the surface was wider than the table had been.

"Moving out?" Priya asked, glancing at the pages.

"Comparing two places. One's eight months, one's a year. I'm trying to work out the real monthly cost with utilities, but the eight-month one I don't have to resign when it ends, it just goes month to month on the same terms, so the term doesn't really matter for the math."

"That's right," she said, stamping his form. "People get worried about that for no reason."

His grandfather stood, hat in hand, and looked at the two circled-and-uncircled totals upside down. "Which one?" he said.

Landon picked up the Gladstone lease, then set it back down and picked up the other one, the laundromat, with its unknown heat. He folded it once, along the line where he had written "call," and put it in his jacket pocket inside his grandfather's envelope of birthday money. "I'm going to ask them what last winter cost," he said, and shook Priya's hand across the counter.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.
story:
Samuel's mother pulled into the far corner of the grocery store lot at seven on a Sunday, where the asphalt sloped gently toward the cart corrals and the only other car was a bakery van with its back doors open. She had chosen the hour deliberately, and she said so twice on the drive over, the way she said most things twice when she was nervous. "Empty lot, Samuel. Best we'll get." He didn't answer, because he was watching the slope. His father, who had driven trucks for eleven years before the office job, used to say that a parking lot is never flat, and Samuel had begun to internalize that, the way he had begun to internalize the feel of the steering wheel going lock to lock without looking at his hands.

What his mother wanted, though she framed it as a gift to him, was her Tuesday evenings back. Every week she drove his aunt Ruth to physical therapy forty minutes away, and every week she came home with a headache and a complaint about the headlights on the parkway. If Samuel passed his test on Thursday, he could share the driving, and she could close her eyes in the passenger seat for once. He knew this because she had mentioned it three times since the test was scheduled, always at the end, always casually, as if it were a footnote rather than the headline.

They set up two shopping carts as the car he would park behind, and a folded umbrella stood in for the one in front. "Pull up even with the cart," his mother said, reading from the state manual on her lap, "then turn the wheel all the way and back up till you're at forty-five degrees." Her voice had the careful flatness of someone reciting something she did not fully understand. Samuel did it twice, badly, clipping the umbrella with the rear tire, then once, well enough that neither of them said anything for a moment.

The trouble was the slope. The lot tilted toward the curb that ran along the cart corral, and each time he finished the park and lifted his foot off the brake, the car eased forward on its own, a slow deliberate drift, and he had to press down again. "It's just gravity," his mother said, which was the kind of statement that explained nothing and somehow still helped. On his fourth attempt he brought the car to rest exactly where he wanted it, close to the curb, front end neatly in, and sat there with the engine idling and his hands still on the wheel, feeling something that was almost competence.

"Which way are your wheels pointing?" his mother asked. She was looking at the manual again, but he had the sense she was testing him rather than reading. He looked down through the windshield as if he could see them, which of course he couldn't. The car faced downhill. There was a curb a foot to his right. He thought about his father's trucks, about wheel chocks, about the way heavy things behaved when you stopped holding them.

"Toward the curb," he said. "If the wheels are toward the curb and the brakes fail, the car rolls into the curb. Not into traffic." He heard his own voice say it and realized he had never actually said it aloud before; he had read it once in the manual, weeks ago, half-asleep, and it had sat in him since, waiting. His mother lowered the booklet and looked at the front wheel, tilted her head, and turned the page to check. "That's it," she said. "Exactly that." He turned the wheel to make it true, and felt the small click of the position settle, and the car sat there against the slope like it had made a decision.

Afterward they drove to the highway, because the test included a merge and the merge frightened him more than any parking maneuver. His mother's plan was the on-ramp by the mall, three lanes, moderate traffic. The trouble with merging, as far as Samuel could tell, was that other drivers were capricious; the same man who slowed to let you in on Tuesday would accelerate to close a gap on Wednesday, and there was no way to know in advance which version of him you were getting. On the ramp he checked the mirror, the blind spot, the mirror again, and a blue hatchback let him in with a small forgiving dip of its headlights, and he was on the highway, doing sixty, his mother saying "good, good, stay in this lane."

He did it four more times, looping off at the next exit and back around, and by the third loop the fear had rearranged itself into something more like attention. He wasn't calm, exactly, but he was no longer guessing. You watched the traffic and made a judgment and committed to it, and if the judgment was wrong you adjusted, and the adjusting was the actual skill, not the judgment. That was not in the manual. His father had a taped index card above his old desk that read, in handwriting Samuel had never been able to date, "Slow is smooth and smooth is fast," and Samuel had always found it a little smug, the kind of epigram that sounds wiser than it is, but somewhere on the fourth loop he thought he understood what it was trying to say and forgave it.

On the drive back to the lot he parked between the two carts one last time, on the slope, close to the curb, and turned the front wheels toward it without being asked. His mother watched him do it and closed the manual. "Tuesday," she said. "Aunt Ruth's appointment is at four. You'd drive there, I'd drive back." He nodded, and left the wheels where they were, and put on the handbrake, and they sat in the idling car in the empty corner of the lot while the bakery van pulled away and the first Sunday shoppers began to arrive.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: The area under the curve y equals x squared, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, is exactly one third.
story:
The library smelled of radiator dust and old glue, and Grayson had claimed the table by the window where the afternoon light came in flat and gray. He spread out a sheet of graph paper he had drawn himself, a parabola copied carefully from the textbook: y equals x squared, running from zero to one, a shallow curve hugging the bottom of the page and then climbing. His calculus test was in four days, and he still did not believe what the book claimed about it. He had underlined the sentence twice and then, feeling ridiculous, underlined it a third time. The area under that curve, from x equals 0 to x equals 1, was exactly one third.

He counted the little squares under the curve. Whole ones first, then the broken ones at the edge, guessing at halves and quarters, tallying in the margin the way his grandfather had taught him two summers ago. His grandfather kept a jar of pencil stubs on the workbench and believed every hard thing could be softened by counting. "Count the squares," the old man had said, showing Grayson how to estimate the paint needed for a crooked wall, the seed for a garden bed. "Count them and then trust your counting." Grayson's tally came to about thirty-four squares, and since the full unit square held a hundred, that was close enough to a third to sting. He had hoped, in some part of himself, that the counting would disagree.

Behind him, two chairs scraped. Priya and Marcus from his class settled at the next table with their review packets, and Priya immediately leaned over his shoulder.

"Is that graph paper? For calculus?"

"Estimating," Grayson said. "Squares under the curve. My grandfather's method."

Marcus picked up the sheet, tilting it toward the window. "That's the most perspicacious thing I've seen all week, and also the slowest. You know the integral does this in one line."

"That's the problem," Grayson said. "It does it in one line and I don't believe it. One line feels like a trick. Counting feels like looking."

Priya sat down across from him, uninvited, which was how she did most things. "So look, then count, then argue with yourself. That's what my sister says college is." She pulled his textbook over and found the antiderivative rules, then turned the page to the section on parametrized curves. "Also, you're going to need this next chapter. When you parametrize a curve, you describe it with a variable instead of y versus x. It's the same curve wearing different clothes."

Grayson copied the integral onto his own paper, the long S-shape of it, the x squared sitting inside, the limits 0 and 1 written small at top and bottom. He worked it through the rule the book gave, arrived at one third, wrote it, and sat back. Then he counted his squares again, more carefully, correcting a tally mark he had doubled. Thirty-three squares and a scrap. One third of a hundred. The two methods had arrived at the same number from opposite directions, one by chopping the world into pieces and adding them up, one by a rule that fell out of symbols like water down a pipe.

"Except the integral is exact," Marcus said, watching his face. "Your squares are you squinting."

"Exact how, though," Grayson said. "I followed the rule and got the answer the book wanted. If I'd gotten something else, I'd have gone back and found my mistake. So did I find out it's one third, or did I find out that I can follow a recipe?" He tapped the graph paper. "My grandfather counted squares on walls for fifty years and his paint never ran short. He trusted the pieces. I want to trust the pieces and the recipe. I just don't know yet what I'm allowed to trust."

Priya had stopped writing her own review. She was quiet for a moment, which was rare enough that Marcus looked up too. "My mom does that," she said. "Physics. She says the curve never touches its asymptote but you still build the whole plane around it." She slid the graph paper back toward him. "Maybe exact isn't the point. Maybe the counting is how you keep yourself honest while the symbols do the fast part."

The radiator ticked. Somewhere behind the shelves a cart of returned books rolled and stopped. Grayson took out a clean sheet and drew the parabola again, but this time he shaded the region beneath it lightly with the side of his pencil, the whole curving wedge of it, and wrote one third beside it in his grandfather's stubby-pencil script, small and square. He would call the old man tonight and tell him the squares had been right, nearly right, right enough. Then, under that, he wrote the integral too, and between the two, nothing, a blank space where the argument between them lived. He looked at the page for a long moment, then folded it in half and put it in his backpack, outer pocket, where he could reach it on the bus.

"Same table tomorrow?" Priya asked, gathering her things as the lights along the ceiling began their warning flicker.

"Bring graph paper," Grayson said. "I want to count the squares under one more curve."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.
story:
Rosalie set the double boiler on the stove before her mother left for the late shift, and by seven the kitchen smelled like a candy shop, which was exactly the problem. She was trying to smell nothing at all. The recipe she'd found online, printed and annotated in her looping hand, said chocolate was chemistry before it was cooking, and chemistry did not care how charming the kitchen smelled. She had a thermometer, a marble slab borrowed from Mrs. Okafor next door, and three hundred grams of dark couverture she had bought with her tutoring money after her father said, gently, that this particular obsession could wait until she was earning.

It could not wait, because Sana's birthday was Saturday, and Sana had announced, in the cafeteria, with the casual cruelty of a best friend, that she was tired of store-bought things. "Anyone can buy a box," she had said. "You're the one who's always going on about process." Rosalie had not gone on about process, exactly, but she had once spent forty minutes explaining why she'd redone a lab three times, so the accusation had landed somewhere near truth.

The first batch seized in the bowl, turning from silk to gravel while she stirred. The second she scorched, misreading the thermometer in the steam. By the third she had learned to be patient with the melt, dragging the spatula slowly, waiting for the temperature to climb like a fever that had to peak. Then came the part the forums argued about: the seeding, the tabling, the arguments about method that people would expatiate on for thousands of words, each convinced their way was the only one. Rosalie had read four of these essays and closed her laptop, because the arguing was the opposite of helpful. What she needed was one true thing to hold onto, and she'd found it buried in a comment thread: properly tempered chocolate shrinks slightly as it sets, which helps it release cleanly from a mould.

That was her test, she decided. Not shine, not the snap, not the folklore. Shrinkage. If the chocolate pulled away from the plastic mould as it hardened, it was real; if it clung, she had failed and would have to begin again with the last of her couverture, which was not enough for a full batch.

She poured the third batch into the moulds, tapped out the bubbles, and slid them into the cool pantry. Then she sat on the kitchen floor with her phone, texting Sana about nothing, about the history quiz, about whether Mr. Iyer would actually collect the outlines he'd assigned, because waiting for chocolate was like waiting for anything: better done while pretending to do something else.

When she checked, forty minutes later, one mould had released. She turned it over, tapped it once, and a bar dropped into her palm with a sound like a knuckle cracking, clean and bright, its surface gleaming even under the pantry's dull bulb. The other mould held fast. She turned it, tapped, tapped harder, and nothing moved; the chocolate was dull where it met the plastic, and when she finally pried a piece out with a knife, it bent rather than snapped and left a smear on the plastic like evidence of a crime. She stood at the counter holding both pieces, one perfect and one ruined, from the same bowl, poured minutes apart, and understood that she had not actually failed or succeeded. She had half succeeded, which was somehow more instructive and more infuriating.

She thought about her father's taxonomy of worthwhile pursuits, the unspoken one: practical things at the top, uncertain things at the bottom, and her chocolate somewhere in the basement beside her abandoned violin and the summer she'd spent learning to juggle. He wasn't cruel about it. He just asked, each time, whether it would lead anywhere, and she never had an answer that satisfied him, because the honest answer was that she didn't make things to arrive somewhere. She made them to find out whether she could. But sitting on the kitchen floor now, she could see his side of it too, could see why a man who worked two jobs might look at a marble slab on loan from a neighbor and see a grandiose production built around a birthday gift, when a card would have done. Both views were true at once, and she could not resolve them, and she found, testing the feeling the way she'd test a temperature, that she didn't entirely want to.

She had maybe a hundred and fifty grams left. Not enough for a full batch of moulds, but enough for one careful attempt, if she was exact. She washed the marble slab, melted the remaining chocolate with the failed pieces stirred back in, and worked it across the cool stone with the spatula, watching for the moment the gloss began to thicken, when the fluid turned fudgy at the edges. Her arms ached. It was past eleven. She brought it back to temperature, poured it into the one clean mould, and set it in the pantry with the discipline of someone who had already learned what impatience cost.

At midnight she turned the mould over and tapped. For a second nothing happened, and she felt the whole evening tilt toward ruin. Then the bar slid free, glossy and whole, and shrank slightly in her palm, smaller than the cavity that had held it, as though it had decided to release itself.

She texted Sana a photo of the bar with no caption, then wrapped it in parchment paper and set it on the counter for morning, next to a note for her father that said only, "Try one. They snap."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: Brown nitrogen dioxide forms colourless dinitrogen tetroxide in an exothermic reaction, so a sealed tube of the gas turns paler when cooled and darker brown when warmed.
story:
Katherine had the practice exam open on the kitchen table and her phone propped against the sugar bowl, replaying the video from the museum field trip. On the screen, a docent in a dour grey uniform held a sealed tube above a beaker of ice water while a cluster of eleventh graders leaned in. The gas inside the tube was brown, the brown of weak tea left steeping too long, and as the tube sank into the ice it began, unmistakably, to pale.

"Rewind it again?" her brother Danny asked, dragging his chair closer with a screech. He had a cold and had been assigned to the kitchen table for quarantine purposes, and he had opinions about everything on her screen.

"You've seen it four times."

"It looks like the tube's emptying. Where does it go?"

"Nowhere. That's the whole point." She said it with more confidence than she had. On Saturday, standing in front of that actual tube with condensation fogging the glass, she had felt something assemble itself in her head, the same click she got when a sentence in an essay finally found its shape. The brown gas was nitrogen dioxide. The colourless stuff it turned into was dinitrogen tetroxide. The reaction between them gave off heat. Cold water pushed it one way, and warm water pushed it back, because when she had watched the docent move the tube into a bath of hot water, the brown had flooded back, deeper than before.

The practice question was the problem. It described a sealed tube of the same gas and asked what happened when it was cooled. Katherine had written, in her first attempt on Sunday, that the mixture would turn darker brown. She had reasoned that cooling slowed everything down, so whatever was happening would simply be less of it, paler by dilution of effort. Mr. Okafor had marked it wrong with a single red slash and written "come see me," and she had not come see him, because she wanted to work it out herself first, which was either discipline or pride and she suspected both.

"Okay," she said, pulling a fresh sheet toward her. "Watch. I'm going to do it out loud so you can catch me if I'm being stupid."

"You're always being stupid," Danny said, but he said it around a spoonful of cereal, which softened it.

"The forward reaction, brown to colourless, gives off heat." She drew two boxes and an arrow, then a second arrow curving back. "So heat is like a product. If I cool the tube down, I'm pulling heat out, and the system makes more of it." She paused. It sounded too tidy, like one of those essay arguments that worked only because she wanted it to. "But that's the thing I got wrong before. I thought cold meant everything slows."

"So which is it?"

She looked at the video, frozen on the pale tube in the ice bath. The evidence was right there, stubborn and uninterested in her reasoning. The tube had gone pale in the cold and dark when it was warmed, which meant cooling pushed toward the colourless side. "It's both, kind of. The molecules slow down, but the balance shifts too, and the shift wins for the colour." She wrote it out: cooled, paler; warmed, darker brown. Then, underneath, the part Mr. Okafor would actually be grading: the system responds to the change by shifting to counteract it.

"That's a dialectic," Danny said, with the authority of a fourteen-year-old who had learned the word two weeks ago in English and deployed it hourly.

"That is not what that word means."

"It's two opposite things fighting and the answer comes out of the fight."

She opened her mouth to correct him and then closed it, because he wasn't entirely wrong, and she hated that. What she liked about the principle was that it wasn't a formula, it was a way of holding two facts in tension: the reaction is exothermic, and the temperature changed, and the answer lives between them. Her history teacher kept telling them to contextualize, to stop treating any single fact as if it stood alone, and she had rolled her eyes at the word every time. Here it actually did something. The reaction couldn't be understood without the tube it was sealed in and the ice it was dunked into.

She rewound the video one more time and watched the brown bloom back into the glass as the docent lifted the tube from the hot water into the air. There was still something she couldn't explain, a layer under the rule she'd written, and she circled her answer lightly in pencil to remind herself to ask about it. But the arrow was pointing the right way now, and tomorrow she would walk to Mr. Okafor's room after last period and put the page on his desk.

"Play the part where it goes dark again," Danny said, chin in his hands. "It looks alive."

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Two parallel plates 0.02 metres apart with 100 volts across them produce an electric field of 5,000 volts per metre between them.
story:
The kitchen table still had flour on it from her mother's baking, so Ella spread her physics worksheet on top of a tea towel. It was Sunday evening, two days before the exam, and the problem on the page showed two parallel plates, 0.02 metres apart, connected to a 100 volt supply. Find the electric field strength at a point between them.

She worked it in pencil. Voltage divided by distance; that much she remembered from the board at school, though Mr. Okafor had written it in a hurry at the end of the period and someone had asked a question she hadn't caught. She set out 100 divided by 2, because the problem also said, in smaller print, 2 centimetres. The answer came out as 50. She wrote it in the box, looked at it, and felt the particular unease of a number that seemed too polite to be true.

Her brother Daniel came in and opened the fridge, which he did whenever he wanted an audience. He was nineteen and a self-declared raconteur, currently between jobs and generous with stories about them. "You look like the equation bit you," he said, pulling out the milk.

"It's this plates question. I got fifty, but Priya texted me something completely different and she's never wrong." Ella turned her phone so he could see. Priya's message read: it should be in the thousands, check your units.

Daniel drank from the carton, which their mother had told him about a hundred times. "Units," he repeated. "That's your whole problem in life, honestly. You read the first number and stop."

She almost threw the tea towel at him. Instead she sat still for a moment and did what her maths teacher had once suggested, which was to introspect before rewriting anything: look at the steps, not the answer. The problem said 0.02 metres. She had used the 2 centimetres line underneath, the helpful conversion someone had printed for convenience, and divided by 2 instead of 0.02. Centimetres were not metres. The gap in her working sat there like a stone in a riverbed, obvious once the water dropped.

She rubbed out the 50 and divided again. 100 divided by 0.02 came out as 5,000. The field between the plates was 5,000 volts per metre, not fifty of anything. Her hundredfold error had come from the unconverted unit, a hundred centimetres hiding inside every metre. She wrote the correct line in pen this time and texted Priya back: got it, five thousand, thanks.

"Five thousand," she said aloud, mostly to the answer. "That's a lot of volts per metre for something the size of a matchbox."

Daniel leaned over her shoulder. "So if the plates were further apart, same battery, the field would be weaker? Like spreading the same hundred volts thinner?"

She hadn't thought of it that way, and she turned it over while he watched, wanting to be sure before she agreed. "Same hundred volts, bigger gap, fewer volts per metre. Yes." It was strange to her that the battery's push and the space it crossed were two separate things, one fixed and the other chosen, and that the field lived in the division between them. She still couldn't picture what the field actually was, only what it did, and she wrote a small question mark in the margin beside the word field, to ask Mr. Okafor on Tuesday.

Their mother came in from the garden with mud on her wrists, complaining that the allotment's lower patch had flooded again, alluvial soil, she said, lovely when it drains and a swamp when it doesn't. She washed her hands at the sink and glanced at the worksheet drying on the towel. "Sorted?" she asked.

"Sorted," Ella said. "Except the part I can't see." She put the question mark in the margin, then took it out again, then put it back, and left the pen lying open beside it.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: A few drops of water in melted chocolate can make it seize into a thick, grainy paste, because the sugar and cocoa particles clump together.
story:
The kitchen at Bellamy's had a smell Morgan could not stop noticing, roasted coffee and brown butter and something darker underneath, like the air itself had been caramelized. She had been hired to wash dishes three nights a week, but the pastry chef, a compact woman named Ilana who moved through the kitchen the way water moves downhill, had caught her lingering at the chocolate station and said, without ceremony, "You want to learn tempering? Show up Saturday at six."

So on Saturday at six Morgan stood at the steel counter with a block of dark chocolate the size of a brick, a serrated knife, and a double boiler already sending up its plume of steam. The restaurant was closed, which made it feel borrowed, like walking through a museum after hours. Ilana set a marble slab beside her and said only, "Chop. Small and even. The pieces melt at the same rate that way."

Morgan chopped. She found she liked the rhythm of it, the knife biting through the block and the shards scattering like dark glass, and she liked even more the question underneath the task. She had read the night before that tempering was not just melting, that it was coaxing the cocoa butter into a particular crystal form, the only one of several that set shiny and snapped cleanly when you broke it. One form out of many. She kept turning that over. How did anyone first discover that chocolate had preferences?

"You're hovering," Ilana said, watching her hold the bowl too close to the steam. "Higher. Or the condensation drips in." Morgan raised the bowl an inch and stirred with a spatula, watching the shards soften into pools, glossy and liquid and the color of something expensive. Ilana drifted off to shape croissant dough across the room, and Morgan was left alone with the chocolate, which felt like being left alone with something alive.

She got it to temperature, or close. Then Ilana called from the dough station, "Seventy percent, right? Pour two thirds onto the marble and work it with the spatula, broad strokes, cool it down, then fold it back." The marble method. Morgan had also watched videos of the seed method, where you hold back a chunk of unmelted chocolate and stir it in slowly, letting it cool the mass from within. Two schools of thought, both swearing by their own. She had lain awake half the night deciding which she trusted, and had chosen the marble because Ilana used it, and because there was something in her that wanted to feel the chocolate change under her own hands rather than wait for a seed to dissolve.

She poured. The ribbon of chocolate spread across the cold slab like a dark tide, and she began the broad strokes, pushing and gathering, pushing and gathering. Under the spatula it thickened and lost its gloss and then, as she folded it back into the warm bowl, regained it, a shine so deep it looked wet. She was leaning over it, delighted, when she saw the steam curling again from the boiler behind her, and noticed a bead of condensation trembling on the rim of the pot.

She did not move fast enough. The bead fell. A few drops, no more, maybe the worth of a splash from a wet fingertip, and she watched the whole bowl of chocolate stiffen in the time it took her to draw a breath. It went thick, then grainy, turning from silk to something like wet sand, the surface dulling as though a light behind it had gone out. "Ilana," she said, and her voice came out smaller than she intended.

Ilana came over, looked into the bowl, and said one word. "Seized." Then, because Morgan was staring at her, she added, almost to herself, "Water. The sugar and cocoa clump together and it grabs onto itself." She did not eulogize the chocolate or sigh over the waste; she simply scraped the stiff mass into a container labeled ganache base and said, "That's how it gets used now. Milk and cream will bring it back, but not for tempering."

Morgan stood there wanting to understand exactly what she had witnessed. She pulled Ilana's stained binder of notes from the shelf and found an index card in small, florid handwriting, all loops and flourishes: a few drops of water in melted chocolate will make it seize into a thick, grainy paste, because the sugar and cocoa particles clump together. She read it twice. Not much water at all. Less than a teaspoon could ruin two pounds. She thought of the steam she had been told to avoid, and of the videos that never mentioned steam, only the infamous drop of water from a washed spoon, and she understood that both were the same enemy arriving by different doors. The marble people and the seed people, she realized, were not really divided at all; they agreed on everything that mattered, which was temperature, patience, and the absolute exclusion of water. Her two schools of thought collapsed into one, and the one had a single commandment.

"Can I try again?" she asked.

Ilana checked the clock, then the block of chocolate remaining on the counter, and cut off a third of it with two efficient strokes. "Chop finer this time," she said. "And keep the bowl high."

Morgan carried the bowl to the far end of the counter, away from the boiler, and set it on a folded towel where no steam could reach. She began to chop, and the first shard rang against the steel. Somewhere behind her, one of the weekend regulars, a florid-faced epicure who took his table by the window every Saturday at noon, was already knocking on the locked front door, an hour early as always, and Ilana was laughing at him through the glass. Morgan smiled, gathered her shards into the clean, dry bowl, and set the water to heat beneath a pot she had wiped twice.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A naive narrator, such as Huck in Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, reports events honestly but misunderstands them, so readers see more than the narrator does.
story:
Kaitlyn had claimed the window seat at eleven in the morning and defended it since noon, wedged between a pillow shaped like a trout and a stack of novels she was supposed to be skimming for her first college seminar. The seminar syllabus called it "Narrative Trust," which sounded like a workshop for paranoiacs. Her sister Delia kept drifting past the nook like a planet with no orbit, until finally she collapsed onto the trout.

"You've read the same page four times," Delia said. "I counted."

"It's not a page, it's a chapter, and I'm rereading it because it's doing something to me and I can't tell what." Kaitlyn held up the battered copy of Huckleberry Finn their uncle had sent with a note that said only, This one will argue with you. "The part where Huck apologizes to Jim. He thinks he's done something shameful."

Delia squinted. "He apologized for playing a trick on the guy, how is that shameful?"

"That's exactly the point. He thinks he's sunk low, humbling himself to an enslaved man, and he's actually being the best he's ever been in the whole book." Kaitlyn flipped back two pages to find the line, tapping it. "The joke is on Huck, and he's the one telling the joke. Except he doesn't know it's a joke. He reports everything straight, like he's filing a police statement about his own soul, and meanwhile I'm over here screaming into a cushion."

Delia took the book and read the page with her eyebrows doing most of the work. She was fourteen and treated Kaitlyn's assignments as personal entertainment, a position Kaitlyn alternately resented and exploited. "So the narrator is lying?"

"No. That's the thing. He's not lying at all. A naive narrator, like Huck, reports events honestly but misunderstands them, so readers see more than the narrator does." Kaitlyn heard herself say it and then heard it again, the way you sometimes only understand a sentence once it's escaped into the room. "He's honest and wrong at the same time. Which is a genuinely terrible combination in a person and a genuinely great one in a book."

Delia licked her thumb and turned a few pages ahead, hunting for something. "Okay, so if he's wrong about the apology, is he wrong about everything else? Like the part where he can't pray."

"Probably wrong a lot. But I can't prove which parts, and that's what's wrecking me." Kaitlyn pulled her knees up. "Our teacher wants us to parametrize trust, basically. Like, you could set a slider for how honest the narrator is and another slider for how much they understand, and Huck maxes out the first one and bottoms out the second. But then there's a third thing I can't make into a slider, which is whether he starts to understand Jim halfway through and then slides backward, or whether he understood all along and the society around him keeps dragging the words out of his mouth."

"That's a lot of sliders for a river book," Delia said. "Also you owe me a soda, I did your dish duty last night while you were out here communing with the trout pillow."

"That wasn't a debt, that was reparation for the time you told Mom I failed my driving test when I hadn't even taken it."

"I told her you would fail it, which was a prediction, and it came true, which makes me a narrator you can trust."

Kaitlyn threw the trout pillow at her, and Delia caught it against her chest like a beloved pet. They sat quietly for a minute, the window fogging faintly where Kaitlyn's tea had been steaming. Outside, the backyard sloped up toward the water tower, and in the low winter light the whole hill looked almost montane, scrubby and cold and grander than a suburban slope had any right to look.

"The funniest parts are the saddest parts," Kaitlyn said. "The duke and the king stuff. He just writes down everything they say, all their fake titles and their speeches, completely deadpan, and it's hilarious because he doesn't clock that they're con men for the longest time. Meanwhile Jim's whole life is at stake in the background."

"So do you write the essay about how funny it is or how sad it is?"

Kaitlyn looked at her margin notes, which had degenerated from analysis into a running argument with herself, arrows circling, one word underlined three times and then crossed out. "Both, I think. And then admit at the end that I can't tell where Huck's blindness ends and mine starts, because maybe I'm trusting him in places I shouldn't and doubting him in places he's earned better. The essay's due Friday and that's a terrible thesis."

"It's fine, you love terrible theses," Delia said, standing, taking the book with her. "Like your eighth-grade one about how the dog dies in every book to teach the dad a lesson."

"That was a strong thesis and I stand by it."

Delia was already at the doorway, Huck held open in one hand, reading with her lips moving. "Hey, Katie," she said, without looking up. "When he apologizes to Jim. Does he say sorry, or does he say he's humble?"

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
story:
The hardware store smelled of cut pine and machine oil, and by four o'clock the light through the front windows had gone the color of weak tea. Carson was restocking bolts by size, a job that required no thought, which was the problem. His economics club met on Thursday nights, and Mr. Ferreira had given them a prompt for the following week: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. Carson had read the chapter twice. He could recite it. He could not quite feel it.

Denny worked the register on Sundays, a pugnacious kid from the vocational school who argued about everything, including things he cared nothing about. When business went quiet he leaned on the counter and talked. Today he had heard about the prompt from Carson's phone screen, glimpsed sideways, and he had opinions.

"Look, it's simple," Denny said, snapping a rubber band around a receipt roll. "Prices go up, the bank goes up. Same amount. Match it. Done." He drew a horizontal line in the air with one finger, then another beside it, level, parallel.

Carson turned a bin of quarter-inch bolts so the labels faced out. "Our club president says it doesn't work like that."

"Then your president is wrong."

"That's what I thought too," Carson said, and this was true, or half true. He had thought it was a matter of matching, of keeping pace, the way you'd raise an umbrella exactly as high as the rain. But Priya, who was going to study economics at State, had drawn two lines on the whiteboard at the last meeting, and the second line had climbed steeper than the first, and she had said something Carson had written on his hand because his notebook was in his bag.

He uncurled his fingers now, in the pine smell, and read the smudged ink. "It's called the Taylor rule," he said aloud, because Priya had said it that way, plainly, the way you'd name a street.

"What's a Taylor?"

"A guy. John Taylor. He proposed it." Carson set down the bolt bin. "And the rule says when inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise the interest rate by more than one percentage point."

Denny squinted at him, waiting for the trick. "More? That's overshooting. That's a thermostat that goes to eighty when you set seventy."

Carson looked at the rows of bolts, graduated from tiny to substantial, each bin holding its own size and no other. Somewhere in the back a saw shrieked and stopped. He was aware that he was standing at the edge of something Priya understood and he did not, that the "more than" adumbrated an idea he couldn't yet see whole, some logic sitting just behind the words like a shape behind frosted glass. He didn't want to pretend at it. He'd done that on the last essay and gotten a B minus and a note in red: assertion without reasoning.

"I don't know why more," he said. "I only know that it is more. Taylor said so, and the club president says the whole point is that matching isn't enough, but she didn't finish the explanation because the bell went."

"So you're going to stand there Thursday and say, it's more because some guy said it's more."

"No." Carson rolled the empty bolt tray back onto its shelf. "I'm going to say what I actually understand, and then say where it stops."

Denny made a low noise, part approval, part contempt. "That's a contrivance. Admitting ignorance so nobody can pin you."

"It's not a contrivance if it's just true," Carson said. "I know inflation goes up one point. I know the rate should go up more than one point. I know the rule has a name. What I don't know yet is why the gap matters, and I'd rather say that out loud than invent something that sounds good." He heard his own voice go steady on the last sentence, steadier than he felt.

A customer came in then, an older woman carrying a broken gate hinge wrapped in a paper towel, and Denny straightened and put on his selling face. While he walked her toward aisle six, Carson stayed by the bolts and held his marked hand under the light. The ink had smeared but the words held. More than one percentage point. Underneath, in smaller letters, he added a question mark, careful, with the tip of a pencil from his shirt pocket, and then he closed his fist gently around it.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Leo arrived at the track at six in the morning with a notebook, a pencil, and the conviction that the next twelve weeks could be reduced to arithmetic. He had found the plan online: a spreadsheet, a pyramid of numbers, each week's mileage rising from the last by exactly one tenth. Week one, thirty kilometers. Week two, thirty-three. He had copied it out carefully, and then transcribed it a second time onto graph paper because the first version had seemed, in some way he couldn't name, sloppy.

Dev was already there, sitting on the infield grass with his shoes off, rubbing his ankle. Dev wanted the same thing Leo wanted, the county final in May, but he wanted it the way you want a person, anxiously, sleeplessly, checking his shins each night for tenderness the way other boys checked their phones.

"You're doing the ten percent thing," Dev said, not a question. He had seen the notebook.

"It's the rule," Leo said. "You never raise your weekly distance more than ten percent. It's how you don't get hurt."

"Whose rule?"

Leo didn't have an answer that satisfied him, so he gave the one he had. "Everybody's. It's everywhere. Every plan uses it."

Dev pulled his shoe back on and stood, wobbling slightly, and they began the warm-up they had finally learned to take seriously, jogging the first curve, then the straight, then a series of lunges that Leo had once considered beneath him. That had been in February, before a hamstring twinge had kept him off the track for nine days and taught him that the body keeps its own accounts.

The problem arrived on Thursday. Leo had reached week five, forty-three and a half kilometers, when his left knee began to complain, a small morose ache behind the kneecap that showed up on the third repetition and stayed through the cooldown. He iced it that night and studied the spreadsheet as if it were a map with a mistake in it. The numbers were correct. He checked them three times. The rule had been followed, and yet here was his knee, filing its objection anyway, which suggested either that his knee was wrong or that the rule was not what he had decided it was.

At the library on Saturday, while Dev was at his sister's recital, Leo searched for the origins of the guideline and found something he hadn't expected. The ten percent rule was popular, endlessly repeated, cited in magazines and passed between runners like scripture, but the studies had not shown it prevented injuries any better than other gradual plans. He sat back in the chair. It wasn't that gradual progression was wrong; it was that this particular number, the one he had treated as a law of nature, was a habit rather than a finding. Other plans, slower in some weeks, steadier in others, did just as well. Nobody had proven the decimal point holy.

He walked to the track in the late afternoon to think it through with his feet, which was the only way he knew how to think. On one side was the version of himself that wanted the season to be governed by a rule, a despot he could obey, because obedience was easier than judgment. On the other side was the messier truth: that the number was a convention, and that he would have to decide, week by week, how his knee felt and what his legs could carry, without the comfort of a formula that had never actually been proven. He ran four easy kilometers and let the two positions argue. By the last lap he had landed somewhere between them, though not comfortably. He would still progress gradually; he would just stop pretending the exact percentage was science.

He found Dev on the bleachers, eating an orange, and told him what he had learned, laying it out plainly: the rule was a popular guideline, but the research hadn't shown it beat other gradual approaches at preventing injuries. Dev was quiet for a while, peeling the last strip of rind.

"So what do we do instead?" Dev asked.

"I don't fully know yet," Leo said, and it was the first honest sentence he had spoken all week. He opened the notebook to a fresh page and wrote at the top, Week six, and left the rest blank. "We build it. Warm-ups, rest days, and mileage I actually choose instead of calculate." Dev leaned over and added a small note beside Monday: ankie, easy. Leo crossed it out and wrote nothing under it, and under Tuesday he wrote rest, and they sat there in the fading light arguing amiably about Wednesday until the groundskeeper called from the fence that the gates were closing.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Chuseok, Korea's harvest festival on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, many families hold charye, a memorial rite that sets out food for their ancestors.
story:
The letter arrived on Tuesday, in the slanted handwriting Parker's grandmother had never bothered to straighten out, and he read it standing in the kitchen with his shoes still on. She wrote that this Chuseok, the harvest festival that falls on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month of the lunar calendar, would be his. Not his mother's, not Aunt Soo's. His. She had held the charye, the memorial rite where food is set out for the ancestors, every year since she was a girl in Jinju, and her knees had informed her, in her words, that the arrangement of dishes on a low table was no longer a task for a woman of eighty-one. She would sit beside him and say nothing unless he asked. She signed it with the single character for grandmother, as she always did, and Parker folded the letter into his back pocket and did not take it out for two days.

He arrived at his grandmother's house on the morning of the festival carrying a notebook in which he had written everything he could remember: the direction the ancestors' portrait faces, the order of the fruits, which side held the rice and which the soup. His cousins were already in the yard, and the smell of steamed rice and braised short ribs drifted from the kitchen where his mother and aunts were arguing, gently, about whether to buy the songpyeon from the bakery that had begun to commodify every traditional food in the neighborhood, stacking it in bright boxes with logos, or to make it by hand the way their mother still insisted on, even now, even with her knees.

"You're leading it," his cousin Minho said in the yard, punching his arm. "Grandma picked you. Not me, and I'm the oldest grandson." Minho was smiling but his voice had a small splinter in it, and Parker, who had spent three years letting Minho go first at everything, found he did not want to give this back.

Inside, the low wooden table stood empty in the front room, and his grandmother sat beside it in her cushioned chair, watching him the way she watched a pot about to boil over. Parker unfolded his notebook. He knew the table was set for the ancestors, that much was clear, but his notes contradicted themselves on the placement. He had written that rice goes on the west and soup on the east, and then, on the next page, the opposite. Two aunts, consulted quietly in the hallway, gave him two different answers, both confident, both certain the other was wrong.

He went back to the front room and stood at the table with the dishes around him on the floor, and asked her. It cost him something to ask, because he had promised himself he would not, because the whole point of the letter was that he could do this himself. "Halmeoni. The rice. Which side?"

She looked at him for a long moment, and then, instead of answering, she said, "Where did your notes come from?" He admitted it: the internet, an old video, a page written by someone he could not identify. She made a sound through her teeth, not quite disapproval, and said, "A stranger on a screen, teaching you your own great-grandparents' table. A pedagogue with no ancestors of his own." Then she pointed, once, at the west side of the table, and turned her face to the window, and Parker understood that this was the last instruction she would give him.

He set the rice on the west. The soup followed east, then the fish, laid whole, then the fruit, and here his memory held firm because he could see her hands from years of standing behind her elbows, stacking the apples highest in the center. The aunts drifted in and stood against the wall. Minho came in last and did not sit. When Parker reached for the songpyeon, the half-moon rice cakes, he found only the bakery box with the logo, the handmade ones still steaming in the kitchen, and Aunt Soo called that he should just use the boxed ones, they were already arranged, it would be faster.

Parker looked at the box. Its cakes were perfect, identical, machine-pressed, and something in him resisted them without being able to say why, the same something that had resisted the letter's handwriting being replaced by a printed card. He carried the box to the kitchen, set it on the counter, and brought back the hand-shaped ones instead, their surfaces uneven, one of them split a little at the seam where his grandmother had pinched the dough. He placed them on the table himself, the split one facing forward, where an ancestor would see it first.

When the table was full, the room went quiet, and Parker realized everyone was waiting for him to begin, and he did not know the order of the bows. His notebook page on the bows was blank. His grandmother's eyes were on the window, turbid with age but steady, and she was not going to help him. Minho stepped forward from the wall.

"I know the bows," Minho said, not smiling now. "You lead. I'll bow with you, behind you, like the rest."

Parker looked at him, and at his grandmother, who had turned from the window at the sound of Minho's voice and was watching them both with an expression he could not fully read, something between grief and satisfaction. He could not tell whether she had planned this, whether the letter had been for him alone or for the two of them together, and he decided, standing there, that he did not need to resolve it. He bowed first, and behind him he heard the whole family lower, one after another, like water finding its level.

When he straightened, his grandmother was reaching her hand toward the table, her fingers hovering an inch above the split songpyeon, and she said, "Your great-grandmother always tore one."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Freezer burn happens when air dries out the surface of frozen food; it makes food tough and tasteless but does not make it unsafe to eat.
story:
The walk-in fridge at Vittorio's breathed cold on the back of Oliver's neck while he counted quarts of stock, and beyond its swinging door the Saturday line was already shouting for the pasta station. He had taken the job to save money for college, but what he wanted now was smaller and nearer: by September, when his mother started her night shifts, he wanted to hand over a freezer full of meals so that she would not live on vending machine sandwiches the way she had last winter. Chef Anaya had agreed to teach him the system she used at home, planning a week on Sunday, shopping once, cooking in batches, and tonight, after close, was the first lesson.

He had brought a notebook with a page ruled into seven columns. Anaya flipped through it without comment, then set a cutting board in front of him and put down a case of chicken thighs. "Planning is a verb," she said. "The list is the last part, not the first." She had him cook one batch of braised thighs, then a pot of beans, then a tray of roasted vegetables, and while everything went she talked about what could be frozen and what could not, about how a restaurant and a household kitchen obeyed different gods, one worshipping freshness and the other worshipping foresight. Oliver tried to hold both ideas at once and wrote them side by side.

At home that week he practiced. He shopped once with a list built from four base recipes, browned meat on Sunday, packed labeled containers, and stacked them in his mother's small chest freezer with the labels facing out. He was proud of the geometry of it, the way a month of dinners fit into a space the size of a suitcase. His younger sister, Priya, watched him from the counter with her chin on her fists and said he had turned into somebody boring, though she said it while eating his test batch of stew, and she asked for seconds.

A message came Thursday from Anaya, folded into the restaurant's group chat by mistake and then sent to him alone, a short note on the back of an invoice he found in his apron pocket. "You left before I could tell you the last thing. Air is the enemy in a home freezer. Get the air out of every container or the surface of the food will dry out. That's what ruins it, not age. Come Sunday and I'll show you how I wrap." He read it twice on the bus, then once more at his stop, and he felt the specific unease of a person who has done something carefully and possibly wrong.

He had used containers with a half inch of air above the stew, because a full container seemed likely to crack. When he opened the first one on Friday night, the surface of the stew was marked with pale, dry patches, grayish white across the beans and one flank of the meat, like frost that had settled and stayed. He touched it with a spoon. It was hard where it should have been soft, and he stood at the counter for a long minute with his phone in his hand, thumb hovering over a search he did not want to make, because he already half knew.

Priya looked over his shoulder and said the word before he could. "That's freezer burn, isn't it." He nodded. He called Anaya, who was in the middle of family dinner and spoke in her brisk way, voluble even over the phone, the sentences coming so fast that he had to write on the freezer lid with a grease pencil. It was air that did it, she said, air drying out the surface of the food, and it made the food tough and tasteless, but it did not make it unsafe. He could still eat it. She hung up before he could ask the question underneath the question, which was whether tough and tasteless food was worth serving to his mother after a twelve-hour shift.

He thawed the container anyway and tasted a spoonful. The broth had gone flat, and the meat had the texture of something that had survived rather than lived. He stood between the trash can and the stove holding the pot, thinking that a restaurant would have thrown it out without ceremony, because a restaurant's whole religion was taste, but a household was a different country with different laws, and waste there meant his mother eating nothing at all on Wednesday. He scooped off the dried layer, and what lay beneath was mostly fine. He rebuilt it with canned tomatoes and a splash of vinegar, tasting as he went, and Priya pronounced it acceptable, which from her was nearly praise.

On Sunday he went back to Vittorio's and told Anaya what he had done, the discarding and the rescue both, and admitted that he still did not know where the line was between salvaging a meal and serving someone something second best. She pressed the stew flat in a bag and folded the plastic down onto the surface of the food, pressing out the air with the edge of her hand, and sealed it. "Even the author of your cookbook doesn't know where your line is," she said. "He calls himself a polymath in the introduction and still wraps everything twice." She handed him the bag. "Take it home. It's your freezer."

Oliver put the bag in his backpack, still cold through the canvas, and rode the bus with it against his knee. At home he found his mother's note on the table saying she had taken a double shift, and he wrote next to it in his own hand, "Stew for Tuesday, the good kind," and drew a box for her to check when she'd eaten it. Then he went to the chest freezer, lifted the lid, and began pulling every container out onto the floor, tearing off the loose lids, folding the plastic down flat against each surface, and pressing until his palms ached.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence.
story:
The Portuguese booth smelled of grilled sardines and wet cardboard, and I had promised Ms. Okonkwo I would do this, so I stood there holding a photocopied article like a man holding a parking ticket he intended to dispute. I had told her, honestly, that my Portuguese was three weeks old and mostly culinary. She had said the festival's language table was exactly for people like me. I chose to believe she meant that generously.

The article had come from a stack at the table, one of four short news pieces they kept for exactly this exercise: read it, then summarize it aloud to whoever was sitting across from you. Across from me sat a woman in her sixties named Dulce, who wore a pin shaped like a rooster and had already corrected my pronunciation of the word for bread, which I considered a peccadillo on her part, not mine. The article's first sentence began with a word I didn't recognize, set off by its own comma, and then a dash of ordinary words about flooding and a bridge.

I skipped the first word. It looked like a name, and names rarely matter, and I was already composing my summary in my head, which is a habit my brother calls arrogant and I call efficient. I had a system for new languages: find the verbs, find the numbers, guess the rest. The system had carried me through Spanish and through one embarrassing semester of French. The system, I want to be clear, was not the problem.

"The story is about a flood," I told Dulce, "in Spain." I had found a word near the bottom that resembled a Spanish province, and I plugged it in with the confidence of a man assembling furniture without the instructions. She set down her cup. She looked at me the way my mother looks at the oven when the smoke alarm has been going off for a while.

"Read the first word again," she said. "Before the first sentence. That is the dateline." She said it flatly, not kindly, not unkindly. "Many news stories begin with a dateline naming the city where the story was reported, placed before the first sentence." I might have argued that she was reciting this like a slogan, except I was too busy staring at the word I had skipped. It was a city. Not in Spain. Not even close to Spain. It was the city the story was reported from, sitting there in plain ink before the sentence I had worked so hard on, and it had been there the entire time, patient as a doorman.

Here is where I have to be honest, because I have told this story twice already and both times I made myself smarter in it. I did not gracefully accept the correction. I said the Spanish-looking word still suggested Spain, and she said a province does not outrank a city that is written down, and I said something about translation being interpretive, and she laughed, one syllable, and pushed the paper back toward me. "Again," she said. "Out loud. Correctly."

I read it again, from the actual beginning. The dateline sat there in front of the first sentence like a key left under the mat, and the flooding and the bridge reorganized themselves around a city I now had to place, which took me a moment and cost me some pride I could spare. When I summarized it the second time, I opened with the city, the way she had opened with the correction, and I felt the summary click into something it had not been before. Not brilliant. Just located. Dulce nodded once, which I later understood was her version of applause.

The festival noise came back to me then: the samba drum two booths over, a kid bargaining loudly in what I think was Tagalog, the sardine smoke drifting gray over the tables. I had walked in feeling fairly blase about the whole assignment, another checkbox for my college application's community involvement line, and I was walking out having learned two things that fought each other. My system, my verb-and-number system, had gotten me ninety percent of the way and then delivered me to the wrong country. Dulce's way, read the first word first, was slower and duller and correct. I still think my system has value. I am less sure than I was this morning that I get to decide when to use which, or that I would notice the moment of choosing. I sat back down at the table and pulled the second article from the stack. This time I read the dateline out loud first, and Dulce poured me a cup of her coffee without being asked.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: In the United States, a 100-year flood zone does not mean a flood every 100 years; it means the area has a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year.
story:
The printer behind the reference desk had been jamming all afternoon, which meant Jackson had forty minutes before his mother picked him up, and the library's single GIS terminal still showed the login screen. He signed in, opened the mapping software, and pulled up the city's floodplain layer the way Mr. Okafor had shown him at the workshop two weeks ago, when he'd been the only teenager in a room of retired planners and one very earnest woman from the county extension office.

The layers loaded slowly, the machine's fan whirring under the desk like something trying to escape. Jackson added the housing layer, and the map bloomed into color: parcels outlined in gray, and over them, a broad blue-green wash spilling across the east side of the city like tea spreading through a paper towel.

"That's the flood zone," he said to Dara, who had come over to watch him with her backpack still on, smelling faintly of the chlorine from morning swim practice. "Watch." He clicked the identify tool and pointed it at a small square of gray inside the blue-green.

"I'm watching. What am I watching for?"

"The house Grandma wants to look at Saturday." He'd found the listing that morning, printed on his mother's slow home printer, the paper still warm when he'd folded it into his pocket. The realtor's description said "quiet street, mature trees, not in a flood zone," which was the part that had made him suspicious, because he'd spent two weeks learning exactly what that phrase was worth.

The parcel he clicked sat squarely inside the blue-green. The panel populated: zone AE, base flood elevation, the works. Dara leaned in, chewing the end of a pen she'd taken from the cup by the terminal without appearing to notice she'd done it.

"So it's in it," she said. "Case closed. Tell your grandma."

"It's not that simple." He turned in the chair, and the plastic squeaked. "The listing says it's just outside a one-hundred-year flood zone. That's the word they use, a hundred-year flood zone. The realtor told my mom on the phone it means the house is safe for a century, basically. Floods once every hundred years, so what are the odds."

Dara stopped chewing the pen. "That sounds made up."

"It sounds made up because it is made up." He pulled up the county's explanatory page, the one he'd found at one in the morning, and read it aloud anyway, because saying it out loud made it realer. "It doesn't mean a flood every hundred years. It means the area has a one percent chance of flooding in any given year."

"One percent." She said it flatly, testing the weight of it. "That's every single year. Forever."

He nodded, then made himself stop nodding, because nodding was not the same as knowing. "But," he said, and he heard how much he wanted the but to matter, "one percent is also genuinely small. My grandmother is seventy-one. She is not, statistically speaking, going to be around for another hundred floods-worth of chances, and she's impecunious enough that this house, at this price, with this yard for her tomatoes, is the only one on the list she can actually afford. So which is it? A trap or a bargain?"

Dara set the pen down on the desk, which struck Jackson as the kind of thing she'd learned from her mother, a hospice social worker who spoke of death the way other people spoke of weather. "Can you do the math?"

He could do some of it. He opened a calculator window, and over the next twenty minutes they worked it out together, Dara catching his errors, the fan still whirring, someone's toddler shrieking joyfully near the picture books. The chance of at least one flood over thirty years came out to something he had to check twice, and then check a third time, because it was larger than either of them had guessed and he didn't trust his own multiplication when it mattered this much.

Then he did something Mr. Okafor hadn't taught him. He overlaid the flood layer not just with parcels but with assessed values, and the pattern showed itself without ceremony: the blue-green covered almost exactly the cheapest housing in the city, block after block of it, the impecunious parts of town spread neatly under the water's statistical shadow, while the hills above stayed dry, gray, and expensive. He thought about the pragmatics of that, the practical logic of who could afford to gamble, and burned with something he didn't yet have a word for, then made himself keep working instead of feeling it.

The printer jammed twice more before it produced his map, both layers, colors banded and slightly crooked. He folded it with the listing into his back pocket as his phone buzzed: his mother, at the curb, two minutes early for once. Outside, the air was cold and smelled like wet leaves, and through the library's glass doors he could see the east side glowing faintly on the terminal someone hadn't logged out.

"Saturday," Dara said, holding the door. "You're going with her?"

"I'm going with her," Jackson said. "With the map." He patted his pocket, and the paper crackled under his hand.

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In translation, the ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain.
story:
Chloe had spread her biology notes across the kitchen table until they covered the placemats, and her brother Danny sat across from her eating cereal at four in the afternoon because he had habituated himself to strange hours since midterms ended. The exam was Monday. The unit was DNA, and the unit was winning.

"Okay," she said. "You're going to learn this with me. If I can explain it to you, I actually know it."

"I'm ten."

"DNA gets copied into this thing called messenger RNA. That's transcription. Then the messenger RNA gets read and turned into protein. That's translation. That's the whole unit. That's it."

Danny spooned up milk. "You said 'it's it' twice."

"Thank you. Focus."
