Their mother came through with a laundry basket and the phone clamped to her shoulder, saying something about a subpoena that had arrived at her office in error, someone else's name on it, and no, she would not drive it over herself, they could send a courier. She set the basket down, looked at the paper landscape of the table, and did not touch any of it.

Chloe started drawing. She drew a long squiggle for the messenger RNA and then, below it, little circles in a row. "Here's what I keep getting wrong," she said. "I know the words but I can't see it happening. Translation is like... it's like reading and building at the same time, and I can't picture the machine that does both."

"You have beads in your room," Danny said. "From the kit Tía Rosa sent."

"So?"

"So use the beads. You always draw stuff when you're stuck."

She stared at him, then got up. In her room the bead kit was under the bed where she had shoved it in March, along with a half-finished friendship bracelet she had no memory of starting. She carried the box downstairs, dumped it on the table, and chose the longest piece of string. She tied one bead on, red, and laid the string along her drawn squiggle.

"Say the pattern out loud," she said. "Red, blue, yellow, blue. Don't stop."

Danny said it, and Chloe threaded the beads one at a time as he read, her fingers moving along the string the way her eyes moved along the drawing. Red, blue, yellow, blue. When he finished, she held up the strand.

"That's a protein," she said. "That whole thing is a protein chain. I'm the thing doing the threading. And the pattern you read out loud, that's the messenger RNA."

"You're the ribosome," Danny said, reading it off her notes upside down. "It says here."

"Wait. Say that again."

"Ribosome. R-I-B-O-S-O-M-E. It's underlined twice."

She looked at the bead strand, then at the paragraph she had read six times without anything entering her. The ribosome moves along the messenger RNA and joins amino acids together with peptide bonds to build a protein chain. The beads were amino acids. The string wasn't string; it was the bonds, the peptide bonds, the connections themselves. The machine and the reader were the same object, and it did not assemble anything off to the side, it assembled as it read.

Danny had watched his sister's face go through several expressions in the space of ten seconds, none of which he could name, though he recognized the general category: the same look she had when a crossword answer arrived all at once. Their sister's moods were mercurial, everyone said so, but Danny had always thought Chloe's were worse because they built slowly and then broke all at once, like weather.

"Can I have the beads back?" he asked.

"In a minute. Read the pattern again but change it. Red, blue, blue."

He read, and she threaded, and the new strand came out different from the first, one bead longer, and she laid the two strands side by side on the table. Same reader, same fingers, different message. That was the point of the whole system, she understood now, or she understood it one layer down from where the exam would probably live, which was its own problem. She still could not say for certain she could reproduce this on paper without the beads. She still did not know why the cell needed two steps instead of one. Something about the nucleus, something she had read and lost.

Their mother came back through, phone gone now, and stopped with her hand on the doorframe. She looked at the beads, the drawings, the two children bent over the table like collaborators.

"What is this?"

"Proteins," Danny said.

She nodded slowly, the way she nodded at most of what Chloe studied, and picked up the laundry basket again. "Dinner at seven. Don't lose those beads in the couch."

Chloe copied the bead strands into her notebook, drawing each circle and labeling it, then drew the squiggle above with its pattern written out in colored pencil. At the bottom she wrote: ribosome moves along mRNA, joins amino acids with peptide bonds, builds protein chain. Then she crossed out nothing, because it was all right, and underlined it a third time anyway. Danny slid one bead out of the box and rolled it under his thumb.

"That one's mine," he said. "The yellow one. I'm keeping it."

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: In the far North Atlantic, the water cools and becomes dense enough to sink, then flows south deep underwater as part of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation.
story:
The map had hung in the hallway of Grandad's house for as long as Victor could remember, laminated and curling at one corner, the North Atlantic drawn in arrows of red and blue like veins under skin. He had walked past it a thousand times on the way to the kitchen without a question in his head. Now he stood in front of it with his phone open to the science museum's animation, because his college interview was in four days and the admissions page said candidates should be ready to discuss "a topic of personal interest," and Victor had realized, with a small cold drop of shame, that he did not actually have one.

He had spent the interview prep trying to invent an interest the way other people padded resumes, and every attempt had felt like prevaricating to a panel of strangers. He had drafted a paragraph about climate policy he half believed and a paragraph about renewable energy he quarter believed. Then his mother had dropped him at Grandad's for the weekend, and there was the map again, red arrows crawling up the American coast and peeling east across the ocean toward Europe, and he had thought, for the first time, that it was odd. Warm water going north. To cold places. Why.

Grandad found him there after lunch, tea in one hand, reading glasses pushed up into his white hair. "You've been standing there an hour," he said. "The kettle's boiled twice."

"Grandad, why is Europe warm? Same latitude as Canada, but London doesn't freeze like Labrador."

"Current," Grandad said, and tapped the red arrows with one thick finger. "Gulf Stream. Carries heat up from the tropics. Any sailor north of the Azores knows it, the water's warmer than it has any right to be." He said it the way he said everything, as settled fact, the way he said the tide turned at half past or that gulls meant weather. Victor had grown up trusting that voice completely, and only lately, reading forums where strangers tore each other's arguments apart over sources, had he begun to wonder whether trust was the same thing as understanding.

He watched the animation again that evening while Grandad watched the news. On the small screen the red ribbon swept north, and then, in the far North Atlantic, near Greenland, it cooled and turned blue and dove, folding down beneath the surface, and the dark line of it ran south, deep underwater, all the way back toward the equator. Victor sat forward. It was not a loop at the top at all; the heat went north, but the water itself sank and came home in the dark. He paused it, rewound, watched the blue dive again.

"You've gone quiet," Grandad said from the armchair.

"It's called the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation," Victor said, reading the caption. "The water cools up there, gets dense, sinks, flows south underneath. That's the whole engine." He hesitated. "But some of the forums say the sinking might slow down someday, and nobody agrees on how much, or how fast. Some say it's already weakening. Some say the models are wrong."

Grandad was quiet long enough that Victor thought he had fallen asleep. Then he said, "I knew a man in the shipyard who'd argue the paint off a wall if you let him. Every crew has one. And every crew has a sycophant who agrees with whatever the loudest one says. Neither of them ever learned anything at sea." He levered himself out of the chair and came to look at the phone screen, blue lines glowing on his face. "So which are you going to be at this interview?"

"Neither. That's the point. The Gulf Stream warms Europe, that part's solid, you've known it your whole life. But the sinking, the overturning, whether it slows, that's where it gets uncertain. I can hold both. The certain part and the uncertain part."

"That's not how I'd have put it at seventeen," Grandad said. "We liked a good answer better than a true one."

They stood together over the phone, the news murmuring about football, the hall map's red arrows pointing steadily northeast behind them. Victor rehearsed it once, out loud, the warm current carrying heat toward Europe, the cooling, the sinking, the deep southward flow, and then the part where he would say, "what happens next, no one knows for certain," and mean it. Grandad listened all the way through without interrupting, which Victor understood was the highest compliment available.

At the door on Sunday, bag over his shoulder, Victor asked, "You must have seen this coming, all those years crossing the Atlantic. The water going down."

Grandad pulled the door shut behind them and looked out at the flat gray sea beyond the garden wall. "Forty years I sailed over that exact spot," he said, "and the only thing I ever noticed there was fog."

"Forty years and you never once felt the water sinking?"

Grandad locked the door and pocketed the key. "I never once thought to ask the ocean a question. That's your job now."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: At a Seder, a piece of the middle matzah called the afikoman is set aside, often hidden for children to find, and eaten as the last food of the meal.
story:
William had agreed to lead the Seder at his Aunt Ruth's house before he understood what he was agreeing to. His grandfather had led it for forty years, and after his death in January, nobody else wanted the job, so it had drifted downhill until it landed on William, who was eighteen and home from his first year of college and, his uncle Martin had said, "young enough to learn the Hebrew properly this time." He had studied the Haggadah for three weeks, memorized the order of the blessings, practiced the four questions with his cousin Dana, who was nine and merciless. What he had not practiced was the physical choreography: the pouring, the covering, the breaking.

The table was set for nineteen when he realized something was missing from his memory of the sequence. He stood at the head of the table with the three sheets of matzah on the seder plate, and he broke the middle one in half as the book instructed, wrapped the larger piece in a napkin, and then stood there holding it with no idea what came next.

"The afikoman," Dana said. "That's the afikoman. You hide it and we find it."

The word unlocked the rest. He remembered his grandfather slipping out of the room, allegedly to use the bathroom, while the children ostentatiously studied their shoes. William had never thought about it as a step he would someday have to perform; it had simply happened, like weather. Now nineteen relatives were watching him hold a wrapped cracker and pretending, out of kindness, to be absorbed in their cups. Uncle Martin, whose bellicose opinions on politics had already ignited twice during the soup, raised an eyebrow. William excused himself, walked into the hallway with exaggerated calm, and realized he had no plan whatsoever.

He hid it behind the books in the sideboard, low, at Dana's eye level, because she had confided in the car that finding it was the only part of the evening she actually liked, and he wanted her to have it. Then he returned to the table and allayed the small worry on his aunt's face with a nod that said everything was under control, which was not true but was necessary.

The meal proceeded. During the food, the argument arrived on schedule: his cousin Nadia, who was studying comparative religion, remarked that the Exodus story framed liberation in a way that had been used to justify everything from abolition to a kind of theocracy, and Martin took this as a personal insult, and for ten minutes the parsley and the salt water sat abandoned while everyone relitigated the meaning of freedom. William let it run longer than he should have, partly because he did not know how to stop it and partly because he wanted to hear where it went. Nadia was right that a story could be turned to any purpose. Martin was right that it had carried people through things Nadia had only read about. William could not see how to hold both at once, so he did what his grandfather had apparently done in such moments, which was to move the table forward.

When it came time, he sent the children hunting. Dana found it in ninety seconds, which was too fast, and she knew it was too fast, and her face fell even as she held up the napkin in triumph. The ransom negotiation, the traditional chaos of it, lifted the room. William broke the recovered matzah into pieces and distributed them, because it had to be eaten as the last food of the meal, nothing after it, a detail he had read at two in the morning and retained only because it struck him as beautiful that the night had to end on that particular taste.

It was while putting the seder plate away, hours later, that he found the other one. Behind the books in the sideboard, deeper in, wedged where nobody's hand had reached in years, was a napkin gone gray with dust, wrapped around a piece of matzah that had hardened into something like stone. His grandfather's handwriting, shaky, was on a slip of paper tucked inside: "For whoever finds this. You still owe me a prize."

William stood in the hallway holding it, listening to the kitchen noise, the relatives arguing pleasantly about who would take home the leftover brisket. His grandfather had hidden an afikoman the last year of his life and died before any child found it, or had hidden it as a joke for some future Passover, and there was no way now to know which, and William understood that he would carry both possibilities without resolving them. He carried the old napkin into the kitchen and set it on the counter in front of Aunt Ruth.

Dana looked at it, then at William, and said, "Does this mean I get two prizes?"

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: A coda is an optional closing section after the recapitulation that reinforces the home key and brings the movement to an end.
story:
The garage still smelled of the lawnmower it had once sheltered, though the lawnmower had been gone two years and a rug, an amp, and a card table had drifted in to fill the space like silt, an alluvial layer of everything Laurie's family didn't want in the house. She had claimed the corner by the freezer for herself: a folding chair, her headphones, a photocopied score of Mozart's K. 332, and a yellow marker going dry in her fist.

She wanted the theory placement for the youth symphony's summer session, and the theory placement wanted, among other indignities, a sonata-form analysis of the first movement. The instructions were brisk. Mark the exposition where the second theme begins, mark the development where the music leaves the home key, mark the recapitulation where the first theme returns and the key is restored. Laurie had done all three. She had even done them correctly, more or less, which surprised her enough that she checked twice.

The problem arrived at measure 194. Her recapitulation bracket closed there, tidy and defensible, and the music kept going. Twelve more measures, insistent and loud, hammering the home key like someone knocking on a door they knew was already open. Laurie counted the measures, then recounted them, then leaned back until the folding chair creaked.

"Your face looks like the music owes you money," said Dex, who had come over to practice drums and had been politely unperfumed by her silence for twenty minutes.

"My markings run out and the piece doesn't," Laurie said. "Either Mozart is wrong or I am, and I don't like my odds."

Dex came over, wiping his hands on his jeans, and looked at the score the way he looked at sheet music generally, which was the way a cat looks at a crossword. "What's the extra part doing?"

"Ending it. It's just, everything I was taught to mark has already happened." She played the section through, mouthing along, and watched the final measures land over and over on the tonic, on the home key, the same note the whole movement had been leaning toward. It wasn't a new theme. It wasn't a development. It came after everything she'd been told mattered, and it existed purely to close.

Her grandmother's neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, had once used the word, at the retirement home where Laurie played for a small honorarium every third Sunday, fifteen dollars and a plate of jollof rice. The word had come up when Mrs. Okafor was talking about her late husband's speeches, which always ran long. "Every piece has one," she'd said, tapping Laurie's forearm with a spoon. "It's a coda." Laurie had assumed it was a literary thing. She hadn't known it belonged to her too, sitting there in the Mozart, optional, after the recapitulation, reinforcing the home key, dragging the movement to its close like a host standing at the door with your coat already in hand.

She wrote coda, small, in pencil, at measure 194, then drew the bracket to the final barline. It was a strange relief. All semester she'd felt that the form was a cage the music had been shoved into, that analysis was the kind of thing people did to stigmatize pleasure, to make listening feel like homework. And maybe it was, partly. But the coda had changed her mind about something, or at least complicated it. The form wasn't only a cage; it was also a set of expectations the music could play with, a promise made so it could be kept, or kept late, or kept with a wink. The hammering at the end wasn't extra. It was the movement taking a breath before it let go.

She wasn't sure she could say that on the placement exam. The exam wanted brackets, and she would give it brackets. The rest she would keep for the garage, where it could sit beside the amp and the dead yellow highlighter and the rug that had been a lawn ornament in a previous life.

Dex had gone back to the kit and was watching her in the mirror they'd bolted to the wall, the mirror that stigmatized nothing and flattered no one. "So is it done?" he asked. "Can I make noise now?"

"One second." Laurie put the score flat on the card table, aligned its edges with the table's, and set the pencil across it like a little roof. "Okay," she said. "Play."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: K. Anders Ericsson and colleagues' 1993 study of violinists described 'deliberate practice': effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback, not just logging hours.
story:
Leo arrived at the field twenty minutes early, before any of the eleven-year-olds could see him standing there without a plan. Saturday's tournament was five days away, and his team, the Ravens, had lost their last three games the same way, by a combined margin of two goals, which meant the problem was not effort. It was passing. They could dribble and they could chase, but the ball died at their feet whenever it had to travel between two of them. The head coach, Mr. Ruiz, had missed two practices in a row for work, leaving Leo with a whistle and a binder and the instruction to "just get them touches." Leo knew what getting them touches looked like: a scrimmage, forty minutes of formless running, the same mistakes at higher speed.

He set down his bag and took out a printout. He'd found it the night before while avoiding his chemistry homework, a stack of enthalpy problems still waiting on his desk at home, calculations about heat absorbed and released that felt simpler than the problem on this grass. The printout was from a study done in 1993 by K. Anders Ericsson and some colleagues, who had looked at violinists. The best ones hadn't just logged hours. They did effortful work on specific weaknesses, and they got immediate feedback, so they knew the instant something went wrong. Leo read the sentence twice on the bench, then folded the paper into his back pocket.

The boys showed up in twos and threes, cleats clacking on the pavement, and immediately began the ritual plea for scrimmage. "We always scrimmage," said Marcus, the smallest and loudest of them. Leo held up his hand. "Not today. Today we fix one thing." A groan traveled down the line of eleven-year-olds like a wave. "We have a game Saturday," Leo said, which didn't allay anything, so he blew the whistle and started them moving before the grumbling could organize itself.

He ran the drill he had drawn in the binder the night before: two lines, ten yards apart, gates of cones between them, and a rule that every ball had to go through a gate to count. First touch out of your feet, head up, pass into the gate. When a pass missed, the ball came back to the same boy immediately, and he tried again while it still stung. It was tedious. It was repetitive. Within fifteen minutes the boys were complaining that it wasn't fun, and Leo had to admit, watching them, that it looked nothing like soccer. He kept blowing the whistle.

By the fourth round, the misses changed. Before, the passes had gone everywhere, astray in every direction at once. Now they missed narrowly, clipped the cone, rolled a foot wide. The errors were shrinking into a pattern. Marcus kept pulling his plant foot open and pushing the ball right of every gate. Leo stopped the line. "Marcus, your toe. Point it at the gate." Marcus missed again, immediately, and corrected himself before Leo could say anything. Then the ball went through.

From the far sideline, Marcus could see the whole drill laid out like a diagram, the two lines, the orange gates, Leo standing at the center circle with his folded paper sticking out of his pocket. Marcus didn't understand why they couldn't just play, like they always had, running and scoring and laughing. But there was something else he didn't understand either: why his passes kept sliding right, and why, once Leo had said one word about his toe, they stopped sliding. It was like the mistake had been invisible and now it wasn't. He went to the back of the line and waited for his turn again, on purpose, which was not a thing he had ever done at practice.

"We doing this Saturday too?" he asked during the water break, squatting beside Leo.

"Tomorrow we scrimmage," Leo said. "But with a rule. Every goal has to start with a pass through a gate."

"That's still a rule."

"That's still a rule."

Marcus chewed the strap of his water bottle. "My brother says pros just play all day and that's why they're good."

Leo took out the printout, then put it back. "There was this study," he said. "Violinists, 1993. The best ones didn't just put in hours. They worked on one specific weakness, hard, and they got told right away when they messed up. It's called deliberate practice."

"We're not violinists."

"You're passing like one."

Marcus laughed, sprayed water, stood up. He wasn't sure he believed it, that boring could beat playing, that a game could be improved in pieces instead of all at once. He lined up, pointed his toe, and hit the ball through the far gate, clean, without a sound off either cone. Leo said nothing, only wrote something in his binder. Marcus looked back at him, then ran to the back of the line to wait for it again.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: At a local maximum of a polynomial the derivative equals zero, because the tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal.
story:
Jessica had promised herself she would learn calculus before September, and she was beginning to suspect she had promised herself this in a moment of unearned optimism. The kitchen table was buried in her half of it: notebook, pencil, the fat textbook she'd bought used from a store that smelled of rain and coffee, and her grandmother's old reading glasses, which she wore now out of superstition more than need. Her brother Marcus sat across from her with his laptop, arguing with someone in a game, his voice rising and falling like weather.

"Could you be less obstreperous for twenty minutes," she said, not looking up. "Some of us are trying to understand polynomials."

"I'm not obstreperous, I'm passionate," Marcus said, but he put on his headphones, and the kitchen went quiet enough that she could hear the fridge humming.

The problem she'd set for herself had come out of the textbook's applications section, which she'd flipped to early because the pure exercises bored her. A small company makes candles, the problem said, and its profit can be modeled by a polynomial in the number of candles produced. Find the production level that maximizes profit. She'd circled it. Her mother ran exactly such a company out of the garage, beeswax candles, and Jessica had spent the summer watching her guess at how many to pour for the farmers market, sometimes selling out by ten, sometimes carrying half her stock home. If the math could tell you the top of the curve, the point where you'd made as much as you could make, that was a thing worth knowing.

First she drew the profit curve, just sketching, letting the pencil wander. Up it went, steep at first, then less steep, then it curled over and slid down the far side. Too few candles and you weren't covering costs; too many and you were drowning in wax. Somewhere in the middle was the peak. Her pencil hovered there. How would you find that point exactly, if the curve were a real formula and not a guess?

She went back to the chapter on derivatives. She'd resisted the word for two days, finding it alphabet soup, but the book kept insisting it was only a machine for slope, a way of asking how fast something is changing at a single point. For a polynomial it was almost embarrassingly mechanical: bring the exponent down, subtract one from it, repeat for every term. She worked the rule on her own profit polynomial, term by term, and got a new, smaller formula. The derivative. She checked it twice. Then she sat with it, because she didn't yet know what it was for.

She looked back at her sketch. At the peak of the curve, the pencil line went flat for an instant, level like the top of a hill before the road tips down the other side. She felt something rearrange itself in her head, the way a word puzzle suddenly resolves. At the top, the slope is zero. Nothing is climbing anymore and nothing has started falling. So the highest point of her profit curve had to be exactly where the slope flattened out, which meant where her derivative equaled zero. She set the little formula equal to zero, solved it, and a single number came out, sitting there on the page like a coin found in a pocket. She plotted it on her sketch. It landed on the peak.

"You're smiling at math," Marcus said, one headphone off. "That's unsettling."

"Mom's always guessing how many candles to make," Jessica said. "There's a way to know. The tangent line at the top of the peak is horizontal, so the derivative there is zero. You solve for that and you've got it." She said it out loud partly to hear whether it still made sense when spoken, and it did, and she noticed that she had spent all of June telling Marcus that calculus was a ritual performed by people who wanted to suffer. She had changed her mind about that somewhere between the slope and the solve, and she thought it was fair to admit it, even to him.

Later that evening her mother came in smelling of beeswax, tired, remonstrating with the dog, who had eaten a wick off the counter. "Bad girl, we talked about this," she was saying, and the dog's tail kept wagging anyway. Jessica slid the notebook across the table. "If you made this many candles," she said, tapping the number, "that's the best you could do, according to this."

Her mother squinted at it. "According to what, exactly?"

"A curve. Your profit curve. I made up the numbers, but if you gave me your real ones, cost of wax, price per candle, I could do it for real." She heard herself and paused, because there was a wobble in it she couldn't ignore, a thing she was still honest enough to name. The real world wasn't a clean polynomial, and the peak might drift with the weather or a rival's sale, and she didn't yet know how much of that the math could absorb. "I'd want to check it against a few weeks of actual sales first," she added. "See how close the curve gets."

Her mother looked at the number, then at her, and pulled out the chair and sat down. "The wax invoices are in the folder by the printer," she said. "Start with July."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: In the United States the Federal Reserve's main policy rate is the federal funds rate, the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves.
story:
The check was for forty dollars, a birthday gift from his grandmother, and Riley had walked to the bank mostly to get out of a house where his mother kept asking whether he'd rehearsed "the economics thing" yet. On Thursday night a Yale alumna was coming to dinner, some volunteer interviewer his mother had tracked down through a friend of a friend, and his mother had decided the dinner would go better if Riley could hold up his end of the conversation. He'd mentioned, once, three months ago, that he'd liked the econ unit in civics. That was all it took. In his mother's economy, a passing interest appreciated into an obligation.

The radio above the teller windows was saying something about the Fed raising rates again, and because he had forty minutes to kill before the bus, Riley leaned in and asked the teller, a woman named Darlene with reading glasses on a chain, which rate the Fed actually set. He'd assumed the Fed set mortgage rates, or the rate on savings accounts, and he'd said as much, mostly to hear how it sounded out loud.

Darlene didn't demur. "The federal funds rate," she said. "It's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." She stamped his deposit slip and slid it back. "Everything else follows from that, more or less. The more or less is where people fight."

He stood there holding his receipt. Overnight loans of reserves. Banks lending to banks, like roommates covering each other until payday. It was smaller than he'd imagined, almost clerical, and yet the radio kept saying it would slow inflation, would cool the whole economy, like a dial in a basement that controlled the weather upstairs. He asked Darlene how a rate between banks slowed down prices at the grocery store, and she smiled the smile of a woman whose queue was getting longer.

Three years earlier, in fifth grade, Riley had won the regional elocution contest with a memorized speech about the water cycle, delivering "evapotranspiration" with a confidence he had not earned. His father, who came to everything and understood roughly half of it, had said afterward, "You sounded like you knew what you were saying," and Riley had felt, even at ten, that this was the wrong standard, and had felt guilty for knowing it was the wrong standard. He thought of that now, standing in the bank. He did not want to sound like he knew. He wanted to know.

In the corner by the doors sat the security guard, Mr. Alvarez, who was supposedly retiring next month and who had once, when Riley was small, let him hold the flashlight on inventory night. Riley asked him, half joking, whether the guard knew how the federal funds rate slowed inflation. Mr. Alvarez turned out the way Mr. Alvarez always did, which was to have been paying attention his whole life. His daughter was a bank examiner. His wife did taxes. He himself, before the knee, had worked twenty-two years in this same branch, and before that, and here Riley actually sat down in the customer chair, four years in the mail room of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia. Not the glamorous part, he said. But you learn what's in the building.

The explanation Riley eventually built, that night at the kitchen table, went like this. When the federal funds rate goes up, borrowing gets more expensive all through the system, and expensive money makes people and businesses slower to spend and build and bid against each other. Spending slows, and prices that were rising because everyone was chasing scarce things stop rising so fast. That was one story. The other story, the one his textbook skated past, was that the people hurt first were the ones with the least, whose wages and rents didn't get to negotiate, and that a tool this blunt was being steered by twelve people in a room with lagged data and their own arguments. Riley's considered position, written on the back of a water bill, was that the tool was real, the logic was sound, and the fairness was an open question he refused to pretend was settled. His mother read it over his shoulder and said it needed more confidence.

The twist arrived with the green beans. The alumna, whose name was Dr. Prem, turned out to be a cardiologist who had chosen medicine precisely because economics had seemed, in her words, "like weather forecasting in a suit." Riley's mother deflated visibly. But at dinner he gave the federal funds rate speech anyway, the overnight loans of reserves, the banks as roommates, the dial in the basement, the twelve people arguing, the blunt instrument falling unevenly, and Dr. Prem set down her fork and said it was the first time anyone had explained it to her at all.

Later, scraping plates, his mother asked if he thought it had gone well, and Riley said he honestly didn't know, and found he didn't mind not knowing. Dr. Prem had left her card on the counter with a note on the back: a book title, underlined twice, and beneath it, "For the parts you said you weren't sure about. Neither am I."

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: Research by Gabriele Wulf found that learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts.
story:
Morgan had spread the whole practice across the backyard like a general planning an invasion, except her army was seven eleven-year-olds who kept asking if they could have popsicles first. cones formed passing lanes on the grass, and a clipboard hung from her wrist with drills numbered one through six, every one of them aimed at the same weakness: the girls could not pass to save their lives. The ball went to feet that weren't there, to space nobody was watching, and once, memorably, to a parked car two yards outside the gym.

"Okay," she said, blowing the whistle she'd bought specifically to feel official. "Drill one. Partner passing. Maya, you're with Priya." She walked the line of pairs, correcting everything she could see. "Bend your wrist when you release. Lock your ankle, Dillon. Inside of the foot, Kelsey, not your toe, your toe is a tragedy."

The corrections piled up like laundry. Kelsey stared at her own foot so hard she forgot the ball was coming and took it off the shin. Dillon, sensitize d now to every joint he possessed, moved like a boy assembled from spare parts. After twenty minutes the passing was, if anything, worse, and the girls had gone sullen in the particular way of children who suspect they are being taught badly and are too polite to say so.

"Water break," Morgan said, and sat down on the porch steps with her clipboard, where her econ notebook lay open to her own handwriting: stagflation, when prices rise and growth stalls at the same time, a thing that shouldn't be able to happen all at once and yet there it was, ugly and stubborn. She stared at the word, then at her clipboard, and had the uncomfortable feeling she was watching it happen on grass. More coaching, worse passing. She was producing stagflation in eleven-year-olds.

Her phone was in her pocket, and she did what she always did when stuck, which was type a half-formed question into the search bar. She'd found a coaching forum this way last month, and tonight she found something better, a summary of research by Gabriele Wulf, who had studied how people learn movement. The line that stopped her was this: learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts. She read it twice. Her entire drill plan was built on body parts. Wrists, ankles, toes, tragedies.

"Everybody back," she called, crossing the yard, and knelt to set a cone in front of Maya's partner. "New rule. Forget your wrist. Forget your ankle exists. When you pass, hit your teammate's hands." She held up her own hands, palms out. "Right here. That's the whole job. The ball goes to the hands, and however your foot wants to accomplish that is its own business."

Priya laughed and said, "Even my feet can figure out where hands are," which was more philosophy than Morgan expected from a fifth grader, but the drill restarted and something changed almost at once. Kelsey, freed from inspecting her own toe, watched Priya's hands and put the ball flat into them. Dillon's pass had actual pace on it. Maya started calling for the ball with her hands up, which the others began copying, a little target rising all over the backyard, and Morgan stood on the sideline feeling like she'd discovered fire, or at least a decent match.

She kept the wrist stuff, though. Twice, when Priya's passes sailed high, Morgan said quietly, "Still the hands, but let the ball come off the ground a little less," and once she saw a release that looked cleaner and thought, without saying anything, that the ankle was probably locked this time. That was the part she couldn't resolve, that the body-part words seemed to help once the target idea had taken hold, or maybe they only seemed to, and she had no way of knowing without another practice, and probably three after that. She wrote on the clipboard, try hands only next week, then underneath, or maybe both, ask around, and underlined nothing, which for her was enormous restraint.

"Same time Thursday," she told the girls as they collected cones, and Maya jogged back for one more pass, hands already up, shouting, "Hit these," from the edge of the yard.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent.
story:
The market opened at seven, and by nine Lea had explained interest rates to a woman selling honey, twice to a man behind the tomato baskets, and once, desperately, to a toddler who had stopped to stare at her. None of it had helped. At noon she was supposed to stand in the community tent and give a five-minute talk for the credit union's scholarship, the one her mother kept calling the difference between State and nowhere, and the prompt was printed on the card in her pocket: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She understood it. She had read four articles and watched two lectures. But every time she opened her mouth the words came out in the wrong order, like furniture carried through a door that was too small.

"You're doing it again," said Ruth, who sold bread at the stall Lea had been hovering near for twenty minutes. "Pacing."

"I have to explain money to strangers in three hours."

"Then explain it to me." Ruth wiped flour off her hands. "I raised four kids through two recessions. I'll tell you if you sound like a person or a textbook."

Lea took a breath and tried. She said that when the central bank raises its rate, borrowing gets more expensive, so people take out fewer loans, so there's less money chasing goods, so prices stop climbing so fast. It came out flat, a list wearing a coat. Ruth shook her head slowly, the way she did when a loaf hadn't risen.

"It's not wrong," Ruth said. "It's just not alive. You're suturing two things together with a thread nobody can see. Make them see the thread."

Lea sat down on a crate. Somewhere behind her a man was shouting about peaches, and the whole market had the warm, alluvial smell of a river valley in August, soil and fruit and rain-dust. She thought about her grandfather, who lived for the market's coffee and would be here within the hour, and about the fight they'd had at his kitchen table last week, when she'd claimed, airily, that central banks had always aimed at some fixed inflation number. He had laughed at her. Then he had gotten out his laptop, typed with two fingers, and made her read the screen aloud: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent. Not ancient history. Not always. Someone, somewhere, had decided to try it, on purpose, the year she was born's opposite.

That was the thread, maybe. Not a law of nature but an invention, an artifice people had built because the older ways kept failing. If it was built, it could be explained the way you explain anything built: what problem it solved, how the parts worked.

"Grandpa," she said when he arrived at ten, holding his coffee. "If I say New Zealand started it, is that right?"

"First country to adopt formal inflation targeting," he said. "Government and Reserve Bank, March 1990, target range of 0 to 2 percent." He sipped. "You looked it up with me. You should remember it."

"I remember. I want to use it. Tell me if this sounds like anything."

She stood between the bread stall and the peach man and tried again, this time starting from the story. Imagine prices climbing and nobody in charge saying what success would even look like, she said, until New Zealand wrote down an actual number, zero to two percent, and made its central bank accountable to it. Then the tool: to get inflation down toward that number, the bank raises the rate it charges, borrowing costs more, loans shrink, spending cools, and prices stop rising so fast. Ruth was nodding. A woman buying sourdough had stopped to listen.

"It's like turning the tap," the woman offered. "Rates up, water down."

"Kind of, except the water is everyone's mortgages at once," Lea said, and heard herself laugh, and heard the small crowd laugh with her.

At noon she stood in the community tent with her hands only slightly shaking and gave the talk, New Zealand first, the number plain on a card she held up, then the chain from a higher rate to slower climbing prices, then the honest part she had decided not to cut: nobody knows exactly how long it takes, and the cooling hurts some people before it helps everyone. When she finished, a judge asked what she'd study. "Economics," she said, surprising herself with how sure it sounded.

Afterward Ruth pressed a loaf into her hands, still warm, and said, "You sawed the thread for us." Lea walked out past the peaches holding the bread against her chest like something earned.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
The chain drill fell apart for the third time in a row, and Hannah crouched behind home plate with her clipboard against her knee, pretending to write something. Nine eleven-year-olds stood in the outfield grass waiting for her verdict, and the verdict she wanted to give was not the one she should give.

She had watched them for two weeks before the league asked her to run practices. Their weakness was specific and stubborn: a throw to a cutoff man on the move. The ball either sailed into the runner's path, which was dangerous, or died short, which was embarrassing. So she had built drills. Cone markers. A bucket of balls. A relay pattern where the second baseman sprinted sideways and the shortstop had to lead him, throwing not to where he was but to where he would be. Every time a throw went wrong she called it out. Flat, she said, or late, or that's at his heels. Every time a throw went right she called that too. Good. Perfect. Again.

By the middle of the second practice, the drill looked clean. Nine throws out of ten arrived on the money. She felt a pride she distrusted, because on Saturday, in the actual game, the same kids had thrown to nobody, to ghosts, to patches of grass where no cutoff man had ever been. She had stood at the fence gripping the chain link and wanting to beseech them through it, as if her voice could travel the ninety feet her instructions apparently couldn't.

On Tuesday she arrived early, before any of them, and sat in the dugout with her phone. She had typed something into the search bar the night before, a phrase she'd half remembered from a documentary about flight simulators, and now she read the results slowly, twice. One line stood out among the paragraphs of jargon. Guidance hypothesis. Feedback after every single attempt could make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helped retention. She read it a third time, then looked out at the empty diamond, the bases still pale from morning rain, and felt the idea rearrange something.

"What's that face," said Marcus, eleven years old and the team's loudest shortstop, dropping his bag on the bench beside her.

"It's called the guidance hypothesis," she said, locking the phone. "I read it this morning."

"Sounds like homework."

"It kind of is."

She did not tell him the rest, and she did not tell Coach Denny either, though he arrived ten minutes later with his thermos and his habit of standing just behind her shoulder. Denny had run the Saturday game from the fence, calling cutoffs for every ball put in play, and the kids had still fallen apart, and Hannah had spent the drive home trying not to think about whose voice they'd been listening to all season. Including hers.

So she changed the practice, and the change felt like a gamble. She put the cones out, set the drill running, and then made herself walk away. She stood by the backstop and kept her mouth shut. The first throw was flat. She let it go. The second died in the grass ten feet short, and Marcus's shoulders tightened as he waited for the word that always came, and no word came, and he threw again, and this time the ball angled ahead of the runner, into the space he was about to occupy. Hannah's fingers ached against the clipboard. It would be so easy to say good, to be the voice under the words, and she made herself stay parsimonious with her praise, one comment in five throws, then one in ten, saying nothing that wasn't worth their depending on.

The kids got louder. That was the strange part. Without her voice filling the gaps they began to fill them themselves, the shortstop holding up two fingers, the second baseman calling cutoff early, a skinny kid named Eli who never spoke asking for the ball twice. Their throws were worse than Tuesday's, noticeably worse, and Hannah had to sit on the fear that she was ruining them, that an aphorism she liked, let them feel it, was just a cover for doing nothing. She had been the one who made the drill look clean with her corrections. The clean was hers, not theirs.

Denny came and stood beside her at the backstop. He watched a throw skip past the cone, and she felt him draw breath.

"Don't," she said, before she could weigh it. Then, more carefully, because he was a volunteer and unpaid and had been doing this for nine years, "Just for this drill. Try it once."

He held his thermos with both hands and said nothing, which she chose to take as agreement, and she knew it was only half agreement, and she let that be uncertain. He had his reasons. She had hers. One of them would turn out to be right and the other wrong, or, more likely, both of them were holding a piece of something, and Saturday would decide nothing cleanly.

She had not told anyone on the field why this mattered so much to her, and she told no one now. Four years ago her own coach had corrected her swing on every pitch of every practice, a running commentary she could still hear when she closed her eyes, and the day he was absent, with a scout in the bleachers, she had stood at the plate and realized she could not feel her own hands. She had quit that spring and told everyone it was her knee. Her mother still believed it was her knee.

"Scrimmage," she called out, walking onto the grass. "Eli, you're playing short. Marcus, you're a runner, full speed, don't be polite." She set a ball on the tee, jogged to the backstop, and put the clipboard down on the bench. Denny stayed where he was, thermos in both hands, silent.

Marcus broke from first on contact. Eli drifted toward the line, and the left fielder scooped the ball, and for one long second, with the whole practice watching and nobody saying a word, Eli had to decide on his own where the runner would be. Hannah held her breath. His arm came through and the ball left his hand, cutting across the grass toward a spot of empty air.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In France, the directly elected president appoints the prime minister, but the National Assembly can force the prime minister's government to resign by passing a censure motion.
story:
The line outside Courtroom 4B began forming at eight, and by eight twenty Kevin had memorized the back of the man ahead of him: a gray suit, a sweat stripe between the shoulder blades, a folder held the way people hold something they are afraid to drop. Kevin had his own folder, and inside it was the sheet he had been studying for three days, a page of notes on heads of government and how they come to power and how they go. His interview for naturalization was at ten fifteen. If the officer asked him a question about civics and he got it wrong, he would come back another day, and another, and his mother had already taken the morning off work twice.

The man in the gray suit turned around. "You look like you're studying for the bar," he said.

"Citizenship." Kevin held up the folder as proof, though the folder proved nothing. "There's a civics part. They ask you questions."

The man nodded slowly, the way people nod at a delay announcement. "My wife did it in 2011. They asked her who signs bills into law. She said the president and froze. Then she said, 'Unless it's a veto,' and the officer laughed and passed her." He turned back around, and Kevin went back to his sheet, which was not really about the United States at all.

Here was his problem, and he knew it was a problem. His notes had wandered. He had started, sensibly, with the American arrangement: a president elected directly, serving a fixed term, removable only through impeachment, which was long and hard and almost never worked. Then he had started comparing, because comparing was how he actually understood things, and somewhere in the comparison his notes had drifted across the Atlantic. In Britain, he had written, the prime minister is not elected by the people at all; the party wins seats and the party leader becomes prime minister, and if the parliament turns on that leader, the government can fall between elections, without any trial, without any crime. Two systems, two logics. He could feel that there was something important in the difference, some idea about trust and time and how much power a voter actually hands over, but he could not yet say what it was, and the interview was in two hours.

"You're muttering," said a voice to his left.

A girl about his age stood there with a clear plastic bag, the kind they made you use instead of a purse, and inside it a paperback and a passport. She had been behind him the whole time, he realized, and he had been mouthing his notes like a man praying.

"Sorry. I'm trying to figure something out before ten fifteen."

"What's at ten fifteen?"

"Either my citizenship or my second attempt at it." He said it lightly, but his hands were not light; they had rolled the folder into a loose tube. She looked at the tube, then at him, and something in her expression made him unroll it flat against his leg.

"What's the thing you're figuring out?" she asked.

He hesitated, because explaining a half-idea is worse than explaining nothing, and then he explained it anyway: the president with his fixed years, the prime minister who can fall any Tuesday. She listened with her chin tipped slightly, the paperback untouched in its bag.

"France," she said.

"What about it?"

"France does both." She said it the way you point out a door someone has been pushing on. "They elect their president directly. The president appoints the prime minister. But the National Assembly, their parliament, can force the prime minister's government out. They pass a censure motion, and the government has to resign." She shrugged. "My dad's French. We argue about it every Christmas."

Kevin stood very still, and the line moved forward without him for a second, and the man in the gray suit glanced back. In his head the two columns of his notes were reorganizing themselves around this new middle column, this thing that was neither one system nor the other. The president chosen by the whole country; the prime minister chosen by the president; and the assembly able to pull the prime minister down anyway. It was not a compromise so much as an admission that two kinds of legitimacy could exist at once and fight inside a single government. He had been thinking of the systems as answers, and now he was thinking of them as arguments that never end.

"But wait," he said. "So who do the French actually hold accountable? If the government resigns, the president just picks someone else, right? The voter didn't pick the prime minister in the first place."

"That," the girl said, "is the Christmas argument. My dad says the voter is playing the long game. I say it's like being handed deterrence instead of control. You can't choose the government, but you can always threaten to take it down." She smiled slightly. "He says I've been reading too much American political science. I say he's axiomatic about parliamentary government. He thinks that's an insult. I looked it up; it isn't."

The line reached the doors. Inside, the hallway smelled of floor wax and old paper, and a marshal was telling people to have their documents ready, and Kevin realized the borders of the morning had quietly narrowed to a single corridor, a single desk, a single officer who would ask him something he could not fully predict. He would not be asked about France. He knew that. The civics questions delimitated a small and knowable country, and he knew that country well enough now. What France had given him was not on any test: it was the beginning of a considered position, that no system escapes the trade, that each one draws the line between stability and accountability somewhere, and that wherever it draws it, someone is standing outside it, muttering into a folder. He slid the sheet back in among his documents, unverified, untested, his.

"You'll pass," the girl said. She was three people behind him now, holding her passport up so the marshal could see the seal on it. "You clearly care more than anyone else in this line."

"Ten fifteen," Kevin said to the marshal, showing his appointment letter.

"Room C. Window two."

He walked down the corridor with the folder pressed flat under his arm, and behind him the girl called out, "Merry Christmas argument," and laughed.

activity: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
knowledge_domain: to analyse the sonata form of a Mozart movement by marking its exposition, development and recapitulation
fact: In the recapitulation, the second theme usually returns in the home key rather than the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began.
story:
Maria spread the photocopy across the piano lid and discovered, with a small groan, that she had left her pencil at home. The music room smelled of cork floor and valve oil, and outside the window the lacrosse team was running drills in the rain, which struck her as a heroic and stupid thing to be doing while she sat indoors arguing with Mozart.

The argument was this: her assignment sheet said the first movement of the sonata in question was in sonata form, with an exposition, a development, and a recapitulation, and her job was to draw lines in the score marking where each section began. She had listened to the recording twice on the bus and had a theory about the exposition, roughly bars one through fifty-six, give or take her own willingness to commit. The development, she suspected, began at the place where the music turned restless and started wandering through keys like someone checking every drawer in the house for keys that were already in her pocket.

"You look like a detective," said Priya from the doorway, shaking rain off her jacket. Priya had agreed to meet her here partly for the company and partly because the music room had the good radiator. "A detective who's lost."

"I'm fine," Maria said, with the dignity of someone who had just been mouthing bar numbers. "I need a pencil, and I need to know where the recapitulation starts, and I need it not to be bar ninety-three."

Priya dug through her bag and produced a pencil chewed at one end, a green felt-tip, and a broken crayon labelled "burnt sienna," offering all three with the flourish of a street vendor. Maria chose the felt-tip. It would look unhinged in the margin of an exam, but she was not thinking about the exam; she was thinking about the second theme, the slinking little tune that arrived around bar twenty and, in a detail she could not stop noticing, did not sound the same the second time she met it.

She set the metronome ticking, found the opening on the piano with two tentative fingers, and played until the second theme arrived. Then she hunted for its later twin. Priya, meanwhile, had installed herself at the radiator and begun to gesticulate along with the metronome like an increasingly ambitious orchestra conductor, which Maria tolerated because Priya's waving arms actually helped her keep count.

"There," Maria said, marking bar ninety-three, where the first theme came back in its original clothes. "Recapitulation." But when she followed the second theme to its return, she stopped, drew a small circle around the key signature, then another circle, then a rectangle of pure green outrage around both. "It moved."

"It moved where?"

"Listen." She played the second theme as it appeared in the exposition, then as it came back in the recapitulation, side by side, and Priya's conducting arms slowed, then dropped. The two versions were the same tune, the same shape, but the second one sat lower, at home, in the key the whole movement had started in. "In the exposition it's up in the dominant," Maria said, mostly to herself. "In the recapitulation it comes back in the home key. So the movement ends settled in the key where it began." She said it again, quieter, because it sounded like a rule someone had handed her, except nobody had; the score had.

Priya peered at the green carnage on the page. "So Mozart was just tidy?"

"No, it's, " Maria began, and then stopped, because she had been about to say it was a contrivance, a machine for leaving home and coming back, and the word felt both exactly right and slightly unfair, like calling a good plot a trick. "It's a contrivance," she said anyway, "but a good one. The whole first half builds the tension of two keys, and the second half resolves it." She hesitated. "Probably. That might be the tidy version. Maybe it's not about tension at all. I don't know what he wanted, and I don't think I'm supposed to pretend I do."

"You're very intransigent about a dead guy," Priya said, poking her in the arm. "He's not going to argue back."

"He's absolutely arguing back. Every time I draw a line he moves it." Maria drew the line anyway, after the development, before the recapitulation, and next to it wrote her one honest sentence in green: the second theme returns in the home key, not the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began. Then, underneath, smaller: but why it satisfies me, I can't say.

Priya leaned over and read it. "You know the exam won't grade the last part."

"The exam's the exam," Maria said. She gathered the pencil crayon and the chewed pencil back into Priya's bag, folded the score, and played the final bars once more, both hands, slow, listening to the music sitting down at last in its own front hallway.

"Same time Thursday?" said Priya, from the doorway.

"Bring two pencils," said Maria.

activity: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
knowledge_domain: to argue both sides of a Supreme Court case about free speech before a mock court
fact: In Texas v. Johnson (1989), the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 that burning the American flag as a political protest is protected symbolic speech.
story:
The printout of Texas v. Johnson was forty-six pages, and Claire had read it three times on the porch of her grandfather's house while the cicadas sawed away in the August heat. Her government teacher had assigned sides by lottery, and Claire had drawn the harder one: she would argue against the flag burner before the mock court in September, against her own instincts, against the ruling itself. The problem was that the ruling had won. She kept circling the top of the first page, where the vote was recorded, five to four, and she could not make those numbers feel like the settled law everyone pretended it was.

Her grandfather came out with two glasses of iced tea and set one beside her chair without asking whether she wanted it. He had flown helicopters in Vietnam for two tours, and a small flag hung from the porch rail where he raised it each morning and lowered it each dusk, folding it into a neat triangle with hands that did not hesitate.

"Still homework," he said. It wasn't a question.

"I have to argue that burning the flag should be illegal. In front of a panel of seniors playing the justices." She held up the printout. "The case is Texas v. Johnson. 1989. The Supreme Court ruled five to four that burning the flag as political protest is protected symbolic speech."

He sat down across from her and looked at the trees for a while. "Five to four," he said finally. "You know what that means."

"That it was close."

"That the best legal minds in the country split down the middle, and the side you're arguing had four of them on it."

She had known that, but hearing him say it rearranged something. All summer she had been treating the assignment as a losing cause, a exercise in defending the indefensible, and now she understood she had been treating the law itself the same way, as a wall when it was more like a door someone had pushed open by a single hand's width. The subtlety of it embarrassed her. She had wanted the case to be simple so that she could be simply right.

"Will you listen to me practice?" she asked.

"I'll do better than that." He set down his tea. "I'll argue the other side."

They started that evening at the kitchen table, her notes on one side, his folding chair pulled up opposite hers. She made her case first: the flag stands for something beyond any one speaker's message, it belongs to everyone, and destroying it to make a point appropriates a symbol that is jointly held. Her grandfather listened with his forearms on the table, then stood and delivered the rebuttal like a man who had been waiting thirty years for the chance. The government cannot decide which symbols are sacred, he said. That is exactly the power the First Amendment exists to prevent. He was better than she expected, and partway through she realized he was using her own phrasing back at her, from an editorial she'd written junior year, the one about school censorship of the student paper that he had clipped and mailed back to her with a sticky note saying "proud of this."

"Did you keep that?" she asked, when he finished.

"I keep everything you write." He said it flatly, and the kitchen went quiet except for the ice settling in the glasses.

They argued every evening for a week. Claire discovered that her strongest material came from the losing side's own dissent, the argument that the flag's unique position in American life underwrote a narrow exception to otherwise broad protections, that some symbols carry a meaning so widely shared that burning one is less like speech and more like a slap. She also discovered, reading deeper, that the majority had a point she could not shake: once the government may protect a symbol from insult, it may protect anything from insult, and the list of protected things would be written by whoever held power. She took both arguments to bed with her and lay awake under the fan, holding them the way you hold two stones of nearly equal weight, one in each hand.

The night before she left for the drive home, her grandfather lowered the flag at dusk while she watched from the steps. His hands went through the same sequence they always did, unhurried, precise, and she thought about what the ritual would mean to someone watching it as pure theater, someone who had never folded one over a coffin.

"You never told me what you actually think," she said. "Which side won, in your head."

He tucked the triangle under his arm and stood there in the fading light. "I think four justices were right, and I think the five had to win anyway." He looked at her. "I don't know how to say it better than that."

She had come wanting him to resolve it, she saw that now, wanting the veteran to hand her either permission or prohibition so the case would stop being double in her hands. He hadn't, and she found she was grateful, because on the drive home tomorrow she would be the only one standing in front of that panel, and whatever she argued would have to be hers, including the parts she still couldn't reconcile.

"Argue it like the vote hasn't happened yet," he said. "Argue like you're the fifth vote either way." He carried the folded flag up the steps past her, into the house, and hung it on the brass hook inside the door.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The World Health Organization recommends adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure.
story:
Simon's problem was not the sphygmomanometer, which he could wrap around an arm and inflate with reasonable dignity, but the number it produced. One hundred and sixty-eight over ninety-five, on Grandpa Lou's wrist, Tuesday night at the kitchen table, while the pot of chicken soup went on bubbling behind them as though nothing had happened.

The school's health elective had a certification test on Friday: take a reading, interpret it, and explain to the examiner how diet and exercise could change it. Miss Okafor had made them practice on each other all week, and Simon's partner, Priya, kept narrating like a nature documentary. "The wild cuff closes in on its prey," she'd said, squeezing the bulb. "Notice how the arteries atrophy from disuse, like the rest of us in gym." That was Priya's whole method: wrong facts delivered with total confidence, which Simon had stopped correcting around October because it was funnier that way.

The blood pressure unit had seemed abstract until Tuesday. Now there was a number attached to a man who salted his soup twice before tasting it, once out of habit and once, he claimed, "for luck."

Grandpa Lou's kitchen was an archive of cans. Wednesday evening Simon sat on the counter with his phone and a can of the soup itself, reading labels aloud like a courtroom clerk. One serving contained eight hundred ninety milligrams of sodium, and the can held two and a half servings. He did the math twice, because the first answer seemed like an accusation.

"Grandpa. The World Health Organization says adults should eat less than two grams of sodium a day for blood pressure. That's less than five grams of salt total." He held up the can. "This is most of it. This one can."

"That seems capricious," Grandpa said, stirring. "How can they set one number for everybody? Your grandmother ate salt like a sailor and lived to ninety."

"That's not a sample size, that's one person."

"One excellent person," Grandpa said, and Simon laughed despite himself, and then went quiet, because a person was exactly the problem. The textbook talked about populations, about averages across millions of hearts, and here was a single heart across the table, eighty-one years old, beating one hundred sixty-eight over ninety-five, loving a food that textbooks would call, if textbooks made jokes, a health food oxymoron. Simon's cupboards at home held his mother's flaxseed and Grandpa's salt shaker, two philosophies sharing one drawer.

He texted Priya that night, and her reply arrived like a ransom note: "test is FRIDAY 9am. you still sound like you think the textbook is a moral judgment. it's not, it's a weather report. you can argue with rain all you want but bring an umbrella." He read it three times. It was the most useful thing anyone had said to him all week, and he hated that slightly, because Priya hadn't even been trying.

Thursday he tried the other direction. He walked the loop behind the school with Grandpa Lou, who complained for the first quarter mile and then, somewhere past the tennis courts, stopped complaining and started telling a story about a girl he'd liked in 1962, and by the end of the mile he was slightly pink and breathing like a man who had done something. Simon took his blood pressure when they got back to the car: one fifty-eight over ninety. Better, but not fixed, and Simon understood suddenly that this was the honest shape of the thing. The reading would move, day to day, can to can, walk to walk, and nobody, not the WHO, not Priya, not Simon with his practiced hands, could promise a particular number on a particular Tuesday.

Friday morning Miss Okafor sat him down across a desk with a practice arm and a clipboard. Simon wrapped the cuff, listened, called the number, and then, when she asked him to interpret, he said, "It's high, and diet changes it, exercise changes it, and the WHO says less than two grams of sodium a day, less than five grams of salt, helps lower blood pressure. But it's a guideline, not a guarantee. One person can sit right under the line and still have a bad morning." Miss Okafor wrote something on her clipboard without expression. Then she set down her pen.

"That," she said, "is the answer I've been waiting three years to hear. Most of them just say 'eat less salt' like it's a punishment from God. You passed. Now go call your grandfather."

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex, published in 1949, contains the line usually translated as 'one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman', arguing that society shapes womanhood.
story:
The bookshop on Miller Street had a reading group that met on Thursdays, and Charlotte had joined it under what she considered a small and forgivable pretense: she had told the owner, Mr. Petrou, that she had read Jane Eyre twice. In truth she had read it once, at fourteen, and had spent most of that reading imagining herself as Jane, which she now suspected was not the same thing at all. Tonight the group was discussing Chapter Twelve, and Charlotte had prepared by reading the chapter four times in the bath, which she felt was spiritually equivalent to a second full reading, if not better.

"You're not born wanting things," said Priya, across the circle of folding chairs. "Or maybe you are. That's the whole fight, isn't it. Does Jane want Mr. Rochester because she's Jane, or because she's a poor governess in 1847 and her options are roughly three?"

"Four," said Mr. Petrou, from behind the till, without looking up. "Governess, teacher, dependency on a relative, or death. It's a rich genre, the death option."

Charlotte had come with a plan. She wanted, very specifically, to say something that made Priya stop mid-sentence and reconsider her entire position, because Priya was a second-year philosophy student who used words like "hegemonic" at the biscuits table, and Charlotte was eighteen and about to start college and did not intend to spend the next three years being the youngest and quietest person in any room. She had a page of notes. The notes were, she admitted to herself, mostly arrows.

"Charlotte," said Priya, because silence at that table functioned as an invitation. "You've been staring at your arrow page for ten minutes."

"Margin notes," said Charlotte, closing the notebook. "A mature reader's apparatus."

She opened the book instead. There was a copy of The Second Sex on the shelf behind her chair, the orange Penguin with the cracked spine, and she had read the famous line in it twenty minutes earlier while pretending to look for the bathroom. Simone de Beauvoir, 1949. One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. She had read it standing up between Poetry and Local Interest, feeling as though she'd shoplifted something she hadn't paid for, which technically she had, intellectually speaking.

"Here's my thing," Charlotte said. "The line from Beauvoir. The Second Sex, 1949. 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' Society shapes womanhood, Beauvoir says, it's not just installed at birth like a factory setting. So when Jane stands at the window in Chapter Twelve and says women feel restless just as men do, and need exercise for their faculties, is that her voice or is it a want she was trained to have? And if it's trained, is it less hers?" She paused. "Because I keep wanting to say trained wants are still real wants. But then the whole marriage plot looks like a contrivance, and I liked the marriage plot, Priya, I liked it at fourteen, and I refuse to be told I was fooled."

Mr. Petrou turned a page of his ledger. "Refusal is also training," he said mildly.

"Absolutely not, you don't get to do the wise bookseller thing, you did it last week." Charlotte pointed at him. "I did the reading."

"You did the reading tonight," said Priya, grinning. "In the bath, I'm guessing. Your hair's still weird on one side."

"That's a styling choice." Charlotte smoothed the flat side. "And it's not germane to Jane Eyre."

"It's completely germane to whether you titrate your convictions down to match your preparation," Priya said, "which, honestly, is kind of the method, and it's not an insult. You start strong, you add the evidence drop by drop until the color holds."

The group had gone quiet in the way it did when two people were actually getting somewhere. An older woman named Ruth, who read every nineteenth-century novel with a pencil and no mercy, leaned forward. "I'll say what nobody's said. My mother wanted the marriage plot too, and she got it, and it was a disaster, and she still re-read the endings. Wants don't have to be good for you to be real. But Beauvoir still gets her point, because where did my mother learn that the disaster ending was romantic? Not from her soul. From the shelf."

"So both," Charlotte said slowly. "Trained and real. Not one or the other."

"Or neither," said Priya, cheerfully wrecking it. "I'm not conceding."

Charlotte laughed, and Ruth took the last biscuit, and Mr. Petrou wrote something in the ledger that was probably not about books at all. On her way out, Charlotte stopped at the shelf between Poetry and Local Interest, took down the orange Penguin, and carried it to the till. She had exactly enough from her birthday. "I'm buying it now," she said, "so next week my moral superiority is fully documented." Mr. Petrou rang it up, wrapped it in yesterday's newspaper, and slid it across the counter to her, and she held it against the flat side of her hair all the way home.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, 'A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks'.
story:
The deadline was midnight, and by four in the afternoon Victoria had already broken the query twice. She sat at her grandfather's rolltop desk with her laptop open beside his old jar of fountain pens, the assignment page glowing in front of her: build two tables, customers and orders, then write a query that returns the customers who never ordered anything. The first part had gone fine. The join itself kept swallowing the very rows she wanted. Every customer with orders appeared; every customer without them vanished, as if not ordering were a kind of nonexistence.

Her grandfather was out in the riparian garden, the strip of tended green he maintained along the river's edge, cutting back the reeds before the first frost. From the window she could see his slow scissors working. He had been a typesetter before retirement, and when she'd arrived that morning he had looked over her shoulder at the screen and said the tables reminded him of ledger pages. Then he had gone back outside, leaving her alone with what he called her machinations, though what she was doing felt less like scheming than like begging a machine to admit that absence could be information.

Because that was the problem, she decided, walking her frustration out to the kitchen and back. The join matched rows to rows. A customer with no orders had no row to match, so the join dropped her, and the query reported a world in which she had never registered at all. Victoria thought of her own college applications, still half-finished on another hard drive, and of how easy it would be for some system somewhere to conclude that silence meant nobody was there.

She tried writing the condition into the WHERE clause and made it worse. She typed the table names in the wrong order, reversed them, reversed them back.
