In her notes she had begun to transliterate the error messages into plain English, copying "JOIN" into her notebook as if it were a foreign alphabet, sounding it out: customer LEFT OUTER JOIN order means keep all of the left table, keep the ghosts, attach whatever matches and leave the rest empty. The rest empty. She stopped with her pen down. Empty was not the same as dropped. The join could carry a row across with a hole in it, if you asked it the right way.

While she waited for the idea to settle, she texted her cousin Marcus, who had taken the course last year, and got back only a smirk emoji and "left join, null check, you'll see." Then, needing to know why the whole thing was built out of tables at all rather than something less stubborn, she searched on her phone and found her way down into the history of it. She had assumed tables were just how software happened to grow, the way her grandfather's reeds grew where they grew. Instead there was a paper. The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks." She read the title twice. Someone had invented this flat, rectangular, quietly ruthless way of holding the world, and he had worked for IBM, and it had started in 1970, in a paper with that calm, astonishing title.

"Codd," she said aloud to the empty kitchen, testing the name. It sounded like a man who would insist that everything fit somewhere.

Back at the desk she wrote it out slowly, saying the parts as if translating for her grandfather: SELECT the customer name FROM customers LEFT JOIN orders ON the matching IDs WHERE the order ID IS NULL. She ran it. The screen returned exactly three names, the three phantoms, Mrs. Okafor and two others, surfacing from the join's kept side with their empty halves showing. Not ordering, it turned out, could be stated, could be printed, could be true. Victoria sat back and looked at the three names for a long moment, honest with herself about what she still didn't understand, why the empty value behaved differently from any value she could type, and whether she could reproduce this at midnight under pressure or had merely been lucky.

At eleven forty she attached the file and pressed submit, then carried her phone out to the garden to show her grandfather the winning query, screen light against the dark river. He held it at arm's length, squinting, and read the three returned names, and then, at the top of the page, the fourth row she had missed entirely: her own name, entered in the customers table during the morning's testing, never having ordered anything. "So the system caught you," he said, handing the phone back. "You're the ghost."

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: If the forward reaction is exothermic, raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, because the system absorbs the added heat by running in reverse.
story:
The tube had been in Grandpa's shed for thirty years, sitting in a cigar box between a spool of solder and a jar of bent nails. Robert found it on the second morning of his visit, when the rain had driven him inside away from the collapsing woodpile. It was sealed glass, thumb-sized, and it held a gas the color of weak tea, though when he tilted it toward the window it looked almost brown, like the last inch of a Coke.

"Careful with that," Grandpa said from the doorway. He said it without alarm, the way he said everything, and Robert noticed he didn't come closer.

"What is it?"

"Something your uncle made before he quit caring about anything. Nitrogen dioxide, sealed up with its other form. Two gases that turn into each other and never finish." Grandpa wiped his hands on a rag that had once been a shirt. "Your grandmother wants the gutters checked. After."

Robert didn't check the gutters for an hour. He held the tube and thought about the poster board sitting in the trunk of his mother's car, the one he'd carried into the gymnasium in April with his chin up. Prediction: heating the reaction vessel increases product yield. The judges had let him run his demo in front of them. He'd warmed his flask in a water bath, watched the solution, and waited for the shift he'd promised. It had gone the wrong way. Not dramatically, not in a way anyone laughed at, but wrong, and he'd stood there and said, "That's, uh, unexpected," and the taller judge had written something down without looking up.

He texted Dana from the back step, rain ticking on the porch roof. Fixing the poster for regionals. Need the demo to work this time.

You sure it can be fixed, she wrote back. Or is the whole thing wrong?

He started to type three different answers and deleted each one. He was tired of equivocating with her, tired of the maybe-it-was-the-concentration, maybe-it-was-the-thermometer dodge he'd been running since April. He put the phone in his pocket and went back to the shed.

Grandpa's kitchen was nearly bare, plates in one cabinet, a kettle, a table with one wobble he'd shimmed with a folded hymnal insert. The house had the stripped, deliberate plainness of a man who had decided what he needed and refused the rest, and Robert had privately nicknamed it the ascetic setup, though never out loud. He filled a drinking glass with ice water and set the tube in it, and set a second tube of the same gas, which Uncle Marcus had apparently made in pairs, into a mug of water he'd boiled on the stove.

He watched. He made himself watch without hoping, which was harder than it sounded.

The cold tube faded first, its tea color thinning toward nothing, like breath fading off glass. The hot tube went the other way, deepening from weak tea to strong, a definite brown, the color of the fumes in the safety films. He swapped them, hot to cold, and the colors swapped too, slowly, like an argument that kept turning itself around. He sat with his notebook and wrote it plainly. The forward reaction makes product, and it gives off heat. When he added heat, he got less product, more reactant. The system ran backward, soaking up what he put in. When he pulled heat out, it ran forward again to replace it. He underlined nothing. He just looked at it.

"Supper's at six," Grandpa said, passing through with the rag over his shoulder. He paused at the two glasses. "Marcus called that Le Chatelier's principle. Frenchman. Said the system pushes back against whatever you do to it." He said it the way he'd say a neighbor's name, no more, and went on to the pantry.

Robert took out his phone and typed to Dana, Not fixed. Reversed. I predicted the wrong direction because I forgot the forward reaction gives off heat. New poster. Then he set the phone face down and picked up the cold tube, which was nearly colorless now, and cupped it in both hands.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Earth's surface gives off heat as infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb much of it and re-emit it in all directions, including back down, which warms the lower atmosphere.
story:
The trail to Painter's Ridge began in Douglas fir shade and ended, three miles later, on a bald shoulder of granite where Luke had promised they would eat lunch by two o'clock, because the last shuttle down the mountain left the trailhead at five and Priya's mother would adjudicate all future hiking privileges based on the outcome. Priya walked behind him with a printout folded into her jacket pocket, a graph she had to understand by Monday and that Luke, having gotten a B-minus on his own attempt last spring, had claimed he could teach her.

"So explain it," Priya said, at the first switchback. "You said you'd explain it on the way up."

"Up is for warming up," Luke said. "The explanation happens at altitude."

"You're stalling."

He was stalling. The graph itself was simple enough, a line that hugged the bottom of the page until about 1950 and then climbed in a curve so smooth it looked drawn by hand, and Priya could read the numbers fine. What she could not do was say why the line mattered, and Luke's B-minus lived exactly there. He had written, on the exam, that greenhouse gases "block heat from escaping, like a lid," and his professor had circled "lid" and written "no" beside it in red, twice, which suggested a certain feeling.

They stopped where a fallen tree crossed the path and Priya held out her hand for the graph. He spread it on the trunk. The paper had been rained on once and dried wavy, a veneer of stiffness over the ink, and the sawtooth inside the curve, the little annual teeth Priya had noticed on the bus, stood up under the light like something you could feel with a thumb.

"Okay," Luke said. "The Earth's surface. It gives off heat. Not sunlight, it's the other kind, infrared."

"Heat is a type of light?"

"Radiation, yeah. Same word as the scary thing, different amount of scary." He pointed down the valley, where the clearcut patches glared pale. "All that ground down there, all day, it's been giving off infrared. Upward. Toward space."

"And it just goes?"

"It would," Luke said, and then stopped, because that was the part where his lid had lived, and he was suddenly unwilling to say it again. He thought about the rock instead, the granite they were standing on, how the slab would still be warm at nine tonight, giving off the day slowly. "No," he said. "It doesn't just go."

Priya waited. A jay came down and considered their backpacks with an expression of professional interest.

"The gases," Luke said. "Carbon dioxide, the stuff on your graph. Water vapor, some others. They absorb the infrared." He picked up a pebble and held it over the graph. "The ground sends heat up, the gas takes it in, and then it re-emits it. All directions. Up, sideways, and down. Back down at the ground."

"So the heat comes back."

"Some of it comes back. So the lower air, the part we breathe, stays warmer than it would if the infrared just left." He heard himself say it and checked it against the red double no. Nothing bounced off a lid. The gas took the heat and threw it every direction, like a crowd throwing back a beach ball, and the more gas, the more beach balls came down. He had been wrong, he realized, in a way that was almost right, which was the most annoying kind of wrong.

"The line goes up," Priya said, "because we put more of the gas in."

"Because we put a lot more in. That's the curve. Every tooth is a year, the whole thing is sixty-some years of somebody measuring it in one place, every hour, which is either dedication or a cry for help."

Priya folded the graph along its old crease. "And the teeth?"

"Seasons," Luke said. "The forest breathes." He was on thin ice here and they both knew it; he had gotten that question half wrong too, and he said so, because pretending otherwise last spring had produced a B-minus and a red no, no.

They climbed the last half mile in the open, the sun flat on the granite, and the rock gave off its stored heat against their legs through their boots. Priya kept saying it back to herself in fragments, ground, infrared, absorbed, re-emitted, all directions, down, lower atmosphere warmer, like a girl memorizing a phone number, and twice she got it wrong in new ways and Luke corrected her without, he hoped, sounding like the lid.

At the top they ate the sandwiches and looked at the haze lying over the valley like a second, man-made sky. "So what still doesn't make sense to you," Priya said, "honestly."

"Whether saying it out loud like this counts as knowing it," Luke said. "I can recite the whole thing and I still can't tell if I understand it or just believe it in a loud voice."

Priya looked at her watch and stood up. "We can be uncertain at a run," she said. "Shuttle's at five."

They ran, and the warm rock of the trail gave off its heat behind them, upward, into the crowded air.

activity: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
knowledge_domain: to check a viral video's source and date with a reverse image search before sharing it
fact: A video cannot be reverse-searched directly by most image engines, so fact-checkers take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead.
story:
The clip arrived at 11:40 on a Tuesday, while Liam was replacing the cracked screen of a Galaxy S9 behind the counter of his uncle's repair shop. In the video, a crowd surged around a burning van, someone shouted in a language Liam didn't recognize, and a caption in bold yellow letters claimed this was happening right now, three streets from the community college where he'd enrolled for the fall. His cousin Dara had sent it to the family group chat with the message everyone needs to see this. His thumb hovered over the forward arrow.

"Not the screen glue again," his uncle said from the back room, misreading the way Liam had gone still. The shop smelled like isopropyl alcohol and the burnt-plastic ghost of some earlier repair; a radio behind the register murmured traffic reports. Liam set the customer's phone in the foam tray and watched the clip a second time. Forty seconds. His heart was doing something he didn't like. Two kids from his graduating class had already replied to the chat with praying emoji and which street exactly.

He typed which street and then deleted it, because he realized he didn't know, and because the van in the video was parked beside a wall covered in ivy, and he could not think of a single ivy-covered wall anywhere near the college. He knew the campus. He'd walked it twice on orientation days, once in rain. There was no ivy. This was a small thing, an idiosyncrasy of the footage, and small things were what his uncle always said you checked first when a phone came in acting strange. You don't assume the motherboard. You check whether the case is pressing the power button.

Liam pulled up an image search engine on the shop's ancient tablet and tried dragging the video file into the search bar. Nothing. He tried the link, then the link plus quotation marks, then three different engines, his movements getting faster and less careful. The tablet fan whirred underpinning his frustration like a small animal. "It won't take a video," he said to the empty shop. "It just won't take a video."

The bell over the door rang, and Marisol came in with her little brother's iPhone in a sandwich bag, its screen spiderwebbed from corner to corner. Marisol had finished her first year at the state university and worked at the library, and Liam had tutored her in trig the year before, so they had that flat, pleasant history. "Is your uncle around," she started, then saw his face. "What happened?"

"Someone posted a video," Liam said. "Says there's a riot near campus. I want to check if it's real before my whole family panics, but I can't search it. The search engines won't take video."

Marisol set the sandwich bag on the counter. "You can't search a video directly," she said. "What the fact-checkers at the library do is take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead." She said it like she was handing him a screwdriver, the way you'd hand over any tool. "Pause it where something identifiable shows. A sign, a building, a face."

Liam paused the clip where the camera swung across a storefront. The frame was blurry, so he stepped back a few seconds and caught a sharper moment: a green awning, a phone number stenciled on the van's door, a distinctive arch in the background. He took a screenshot, then two more from other moments, the way you'd take multiple samples. The first screenshot returned nothing useful. The second returned a match from an image search, an article dated fourteen months earlier, from a city in another country entirely, about a truck accident during a heat wave protest. The arch was the same. The awning was the same green.

"So it's old," Liam said slowly. "It's from last year, and it's not even here."

"Or that article used an old video too," Marisol said. "That happens. One match doesn't finish it. Check the other screenshots, and look at when the earliest posts of the clip appeared."

He searched the third screenshot and found a news agency's fact-check page, which had traced the same footage to a local report from the other country, filmed during that protest. The earliest copy Liam could find on any social platform had been posted nine hours ago by an account with no history and a stock-photo profile picture. He sat back. The evidence didn't feel like a door slamming shut; it felt like four separate handrails, each one holding weight. He thought about how he'd wanted to forward it, how the wanting had felt like being helpful, urgent, part of something, and how that wanting had nothing to do with whether the video was true.

He typed into the family chat: it's from a protest in another country over a year ago, not near campus. Screenshot of the fact-check attached. Then, because Dara could get truculent when corrected in front of the aunts, he added a second message: I only knew because I got lucky with the search. Could've been me forwarding it.

Dara replied with a thumbs up and, a minute later, a private message: how did you even find that. Liam started typing an answer, stopped, and looked at the customer's half-repaired phone in its foam tray. He took a picture of the ivy frame instead and sent that, with the words: pause the video, screenshot the frame, search the image. Then he picked up the spudger, seated the new screen ribbon into its connector, and pressed the power button to watch the display bloom back to life.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: Minnesota's Department of Transportation says the zipper merge, using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent.
story:
The laundromat on Fairview Avenue smelled like burnt lint and lemon detergent, and Sara had claimed the plastic chair by the window because from there she could see the parking lot, where her mother's Corolla sat waiting like a patient dog. Her road test was in nine days. Between loads she went out with a rolled gym sock and practiced laying it on the passenger seat, then reaching over to check her blind spot, then pulling the sock back, because the examiner would watch her head turn and not just her eyes flick to the mirror.

Her mother's approach to driving was a single maxim, delivered the way you'd hand down a recipe: merge early, be polite. Sara had absorbed it the way she'd absorbed the recipe for scalloped potatoes, without examination, and for years it had sat in her as though it were law rather than preference. The socks tumbled in the dryer behind her now, thumping like a slow heartbeat, while she sat with her phone and read the state Department of Transportation's page on work zones, mostly to avoid thinking about the parallel parking she still couldn't do.

The construction on Highway 36 was the real problem. Her test route ran through it, and her mother insisted she get over into the open lane a half mile before the merge, which in afternoon traffic meant sitting in a queue while the closed lane stretched empty beside her, taunting. Sara had done exactly that on Tuesday, and a pickup had roared past in the empty lane, and her mother had said, "Some people," with such certainty that Sara felt disaffected from her own doubts, as if questioning the early merge were a small act of treason.

The state's page said otherwise. It said Minnesota's Department of Transportation recommends using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, and it called that the zipper merge. It said the zipper merge can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. Sara read the line twice, then a third time, holding the phone at an angle against the window glare. Forty percent. She had no image for what that meant in cars, so she tried to reify it, to make the abstraction solid: if the line she'd sat in on Tuesday had been ten blocks, it could have been six. Whole intersections freed up. People who would have missed a green light getting home.

A man folding towels two machines over noticed her frowning at the phone. "You look like you're doing taxes," he said. He had a gray ponytail and was folding with unusual precision, corners matched to corners.

"Driving test," Sara said. "There's construction on my route and everybody says merge early, but the state says wait and take turns at the end. They call it the zipper merge." She turned the screen toward him. "It can cut the backup by like forty percent."

"Huh," he said. "So everyone being polite is making it worse."

"I don't know if it's worse," Sara said, and realized she meant it. "It feels worse to wait. You feel like a cheat driving down the empty lane. But it's not cheating if everyone's supposed to do it."

Her mother arrived at four to help fold, and Sara raised it on the drive home, carefully, the way you'd test a frozen lake. Her mother's jaw set. "If everybody merged early there'd be no problem at all."

"There'd still be a backup," Sara said. "Just a longer one." She didn't push further. Her mother had driven thirty years without a single accident, and Sara was seventeen with a gym sock standing in for a passenger, and it occurred to her that experience and information were two different currencies, and she wasn't sure which one the road took.

They practiced parallel parking in the church lot on Spruce Street, between her mother's car and a row of battered orange cones Sara had borrowed from the community center. First attempt, she clipped a cone and sent it rolling like a severed head. "That cone had a family," her mother said, deadpan, and Sara laughed so hard she had to put the car in park. Second attempt she over-corrected and ended up facing the cones at a diagonal, close to the curb but philosophically confused. Third attempt, hands at ten and two, reversing until the cone vanished from the rear window, one full turn of the wheel, back until the front cone lined up with her shoulder, the other way, and the Corolla slid into the space with a foot to spare on either side. Her mother said nothing, which was her highest praise.

Saturday they drove the test route, and when the orange signs appeared on Highway 36, Sara stayed in the closing lane. Her mother's hand tightened on the armrest. Cars passed them in the right lane, slow and orderly, and at the merge point a hatchback flashed its lights and let her in, one car, one at a time, like teeth closing. Sara lifted two fingers off the wheel in thanks. Behind her the line of cars kept alternating, and ahead the backup was shorter than she'd ever seen it, though she couldn't say how much, and her mother said, quietly, almost to herself, "Well," and then said nothing else the rest of the way to the exit.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Code-switching is moving between two languages within one conversation; it is common among fluent bilinguals and is not by itself a sign of weak skill.
story:
Amelia had signed the card at the language booth mostly to get the free cloth bookmark, and only afterward understood what she had agreed to: five minutes, on the stage under the paper lanterns, debating whether the city should cut its arts budget to fund housing, entirely in Mandarin. She had studied for three years, but three years of classroom sentence drills had not prepared her for a microphone and an audience eating skewered squid twenty feet away.

She found her assigned partner behind the tea stand, a boy named Deshawn from the bilingual school across town, who was fanning himself with the debate topic sheet. "You're the one who signed up late," he said. "Good. You can take the opening. I'll do rebuttal." He made it sound like a mercy, though she suspected it was strategy: an unprepared partner spends her minutes collapsing while he sweeps in at the end.

They had forty minutes to prepare. Amelia argued, in her careful textbook Chinese, that housing came first, that a person needs walls before she needs murals. Deshawn pushed back in quick, loose Mandarin she could barely follow, and when she asked him to slow down he switched to English without seeming to notice, then back again, sometimes in the same sentence, the way her aunt did on the phone. "You keep doing that," Amelia said.

"Doing what?"

"Going between the two. Mid-sentence."

He shrugged, still fanning himself. "That's just code-switching. Everybody fluent does it. It doesn't mean your Chinese is bad." She wanted to believe him, because in the last ten minutes she had caught herself doing it too, English words surfacing whenever the Mandarin ran thin, like reflexes her mouth reached for on its own. She wrote her notes in characters anyway, all of them, refusing herself the escape hatch, and told herself the discipline would hold.

It did not entirely hold. On stage, under lights strung between two poles, she got through her first argument cleanly, and then a man in the second row raised his hand for the cross-examination period and asked something about property taxes that dismantled her vocabulary. She heard herself say "the revenue, I mean the money, the revenue," and a ripple of laughter went through the crowd, kind or otherwise she could not tell. Her face went hot. The moderator, an older woman in a silk jacket, leaned toward the microphone and said, kindly but audibly, "English words will not count toward your five minutes."

Afterward Amelia sat on the curb by the food stalls, working through a paper boat of rice the way other people worked through a problem, methodically, without pleasure. Deshawn found her there. "You lost the thread in cross-ex," he said, sitting down without being invited. "But your opening was better than mine would've been. The walls-before-murals thing. That was good."

"It fell apart."

"It switched. It's not the same as falling apart." He tore the top off her boat and stole some rice, and she let him, because it seemed like the price of the conversation. "My grandmother does it constantly. She'll say half a sentence in Cantonese and finish it in English and no one in my house thinks she's stupid. But the moderator's right too. Under the rules, only one language counts. So you practice holding one track for five minutes. That's a different skill."

Amelia turned that over while a group of dancers in embroidered jackets noisily assembled near the stage, their drums already rumbling under the announcement for the next act. Two things could both be true, she decided: that her slipping was not evidence of failure, and that the rules of this particular stage demanded a fluency she did not have yet, a single-rail fluency that would atrophy, she suspected, if she avoided the English crutch for a year and then lost her nerve and never went back up. Her position on the arts budget had wobbled too, somewhere between Deshawn's argument that a festival like this one was proof the arts fed people in their own way and her own stubborn insistence on walls. She had ended her rebuttal, haltingly, by conceding that both mattered and proposing a split no council would ever adopt, and she could not tell whether that was wisdom or cowardice.

"Next one's in October," Deshawn said, standing, brushing rice off his jeans. "The school tournament. You'd be my actual partner, not a walk-in." The drums started in earnest, and behind him the aesthete running the calligraphy booth was arguing with a volunteer about whether the lanterns hung at the right height, both of them gesturing up into the dusk. Amelia looked at the stage, then at the sign-up table, where the woman in the silk jacket was already pinning up a fresh sheet for the next debate. "Save me a slot," she said, and got up before she could think better of it.

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The US Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022 and reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent in July 2023.
story:
Vanessa had promised her mother she would come to the bank on Saturday, and the promise was the reason she was still in the economics classroom at four o'clock, rewriting an index card she had already rewritten twice. Her mother wanted to compare mortgage offers and had said, half joking, that Vanessa was the one in the family taking economics. That was in September. Since then the assignment had landed on the class like weather: each student had to stand up on Friday and explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation, in plain words, for a hypothetical listener who knew nothing.

The hypothetical listener was the problem. Vanessa could recite the chain in her sleep. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, so households buy fewer houses and cars, so demand falls, so prices stop climbing so fast. But reciting was not explaining, and she knew the difference because of what had happened to Priya last week. Priya had stood at the whiteboard and delivered a flawless paragraph, and Mr. Okafor had said only, "Now say it to your grandmother," and Priya had gone blank. Vanessa did not want to go blank in front of thirty people. More than that, she did not want to go blank at the bank, in front of her mother and a loan officer with a tie, on the biggest purchase her family had ever considered.

She tried it out on Luis, who sat across from her dismantling a pen. "Rates today are so different from a few years ago," she began. "Why?" Luis expostulated, waving the pen spring at her, "That's what I keep asking my parents. They refinanced when money was basically free and now they act like I personally set the rates." Vanessa laughed, then stopped laughing, because the numbers were sitting in her notes and she had not yet made them speak. She copied them onto the fresh card in her smallest, most careful hand: the Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022, and by July 2023 it had reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent. That was not a mechanism. That was history. But history was what her mother would be holding in her hand on Saturday, a printed offer sheet with a rate that would have looked impossible three years earlier.

Friday came. Vanessa was third, after a boy who mumbled about "cooling the economy" as though it were soup. She stood, and she did not look at Mr. Okafor. She looked at the back wall and pretended it was the bank lobby, vinyl chairs, her mother's good coat.

"Pretend I'm at the bank with my mom," she said. "She's looking at mortgage offers and she asks why the rates are so different from a few years ago. So I'd tell her the Fed started raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022, and by July 2023 it was between 5.25 and 5.50 percent. Then she'd ask what that has to do with a mortgage. And I'd say the Fed's rate is the price of money itself. When money gets expensive, everything bought with borrowed money gets expensive too. People take out fewer loans. They buy less. When buyers pull back, sellers can't keep pushing prices up, and inflation slows. It's like the Fed turning down the temperature in a house where everyone has been fighting over the thermostat."

She heard herself say it and it sounded simple, which frightened her, because simple things were the ones she usually got wrong. Mr. Okafor asked one question: where does it hurt? She said, "Borrowers first. Anyone renewing, anyone starting out. It slows the whole economy on purpose, and the Fed decides how much pain is worth it." He nodded once and wrote something, and she sat down before her knees could change their minds.

That was the classroom, and it went well, and it is where Vanessa's part of this story would like to end. But at the back of the room, in the chair reserved for the teacher who was observing that period, sat Ms. Adeyemi from the counseling office, and she had not come to grade economics.

She had come because of a phone call. Vanessa's mother had called the school on Wednesday, quiet and hurried, asking whether students could access copies of their transcripts before the semester ended. Ms. Adeyemi had recognized the surname, had pulled the file, and had seen what Vanessa did not know anyone had seen: the withdrawal from the private college with the early scholarship, logged in August, and then nothing. A gap year, the file said, in the mother's handwriting on a form. Ms. Adeyemi suspected, from the sound of the phone call and the mortgage question underneath it, that the gap year was a polite word for something else. She watched the girl explain interest rates with an incisiveness that made the other students sit still, watched her say it's like turning down the temperature, and thought: this one has already taught herself the cost of borrowed money in a way no class covers.

When the bell rang, Ms. Adeyemi caught her in the hallway, near the trophy case. "Your presentation," she said. "Are you giving it anywhere else?" Vanessa said, "The bank. Saturday. My mom's refinancing." She said it lightly, the way you hand someone a fact that is not the whole fact. Ms. Adeyemi did not offer the bromide about doors opening and closing, though it rose to her mouth. Instead she said, "If you ever want to talk about next year, my door's open."

Vanessa said thank you and walked on, card in her pocket, numbers still legible under her thumb where she had pressed too hard with the pen. At the corner of the corridor she stopped, took out her phone, and texted her mother: still good for Saturday? bring the offers from three years ago too. She stood looking at the screen until the three dots appeared.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: A NOT IN subquery returns no rows at all if the subquery's list contains even one NULL, a common trap when searching for missing matches.
story:
The shop sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered nail salon, and Mackenzie had worked the front counter for six weeks, taking in phones with cracked screens and logging each one into the database her boss's nephew had built two summers ago. The nephew had gone off to a bootcamp and stopped answering emails, so when the owner, Deshawn, needed to know which customers had never picked up an order, the question landed on her.

"You took a class," Deshawn said. He said it the way he said most things, flat, as if stating a price. "One semester of computers. That's more than me."

One semester, and most of it spreadsheet work. But the shop's system ran on something called SQL, and she had a phone open under the counter to a tutorial site, and a query that almost worked. There was a table of customers and a table of orders. She wanted the customers who appeared in the first table and not in the second. The tutorial called this finding missing matches. She wrote it on Tuesday night at the little desk in her room, the screen light falling through the diaphanous curtain her mother had hung instead of blinds, and the query returned four names. She printed them on the shop's ancient receipt printer, because Deshawn trusted paper.

On Thursday he called from the back room, where he was trying to suture a ribbon cable back onto a water-damaged logic board, his term for it, held with Kapton tape and patience. "Mackenzie. It's wrong. I called two of these people and they've got orders in the system. Sitting right there."

She came back and looked. He was right. One of the four names belonged to a woman with a pending screen replacement, order number in the orders table, plain as anything. Her query had said the woman ordered nothing. She stood there while a customer at the counter waited to pay twelve dollars for a charger, and after she rang him up she pulled the query up again and stared at it.

She ran it in pieces. She ran the inner part alone, the list of customer IDs from the orders table, and counted the rows. Then she compared it to what she expected, and found one more row than there should have been. The last row said NULL. Someone, at some point, had saved an order with the customer field left blank. She remembered the day, actually: a Saturday rush, a walk-in who wouldn't give his name, Deshawn saying just put it in, we'll fix the record later. Nobody had fixed the record.

She deleted the NULL row the honest way first, finding the blank order and attaching a name to it, a walk-in named R. Osei who had paid cash. Then she reran her query. The list came back different, shorter, correct as far as she could verify by hand. She reran the original query with the blank still in place, on a copy of the data, and got nothing. Not four wrong names. Nothing at all, zero rows, where before there had been four. The blank had swallowed the whole result.

She sat with that for a while, because it did not seem like something a list should be able to do. One empty value, and the question stopped being answered at all. She thought of her mother's church, the one her aunt ran like a small theocracy, where a single doubt in the room could end the whole evening's testimony. She didn't like that she thought of it, and she didn't entirely trust the comparison, but it stayed in her head anyway.

"Deshawn," she called to the back. "Come look at this." She showed him the two runs, side by side. "A NOT IN subquery returns no rows at all if the list has even one NULL," she said. "That's the trap. That's what it's called in the docs, a trap. Somebody saved an order with a blank customer, and the whole query came back empty."

He leaned on the counter and read both screens twice. "So the list was broken before, with the four names, and broken after, with none."

"Right. Both wrong, in different directions."

"So which is it now?"

"Now it's right, but only because I fixed the blank by hand. If another one gets saved, it breaks again. I don't know how to stop that yet." She pulled the receipt printer closer and tore off the fresh list, four names that checked out, two of them people she recognized. "You could call these two today. The other two I'd email."

He folded the paper into his shirt pocket and went back to the ribbon cable. Mackenzie opened a new tab next to the tutorial, one with the database's own documentation in it, and started typing.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP.
story:
The trail behind the reservoir climbed in short switchbacks, and Victoria stopped at the second bend because her brother had promised to quiz her there, at the flat rock shaped like a dinner plate. Theo was twenty and impecunious in the way college students were, which was why he tutored her for free instead of the twelve dollars an hour the student center charged, and why the quizzing happened outdoors, where nobody had to buy anything. She spread her notebook on the rock and uncapped a marker. "Draw me a cell," he said. "Just the outline. Then tell me where everything goes."

She drew a lopsided circle and began filling it: a nucleus like a plum, then a scattering of kidney beans for mitochondria. He crouched beside her and pointed at the beans. "Start there. Glucose comes in, what happens?" She bent over the diagram, tongue between her teeth, and wrote GLYCOLYSIS with an arrow pointing straight into the nearest bean, because the whole unit was called cellular respiration and the mitochondria were the power plants, and where else would a power plant take its fuel. Theo didn't say anything, which was worse than saying something.

She thought back to Tuesday, to the classroom with its smell of disinfectant and the quiz she had failed, the one that had started all this. Ms. Okafor had asked her at the board where the process began and she had stood with the chalk hovering over her drawing of a mitochondrion, and the hovering had gone on so long that a boy in the second row laughed, and she had written the arrow anyway, into the bean, into the wrongness. That was the day she decided she would learn it so thoroughly that hovering would never happen again. It was also the day she began to suspect that biology might be less like a diagram and more like a trail, where a path branched before you expected it to.

"Say it out loud," Theo said now, tapping the rock. "Use the diagram." She pointed at her arrow and recited what she'd memorized from the textbook, and when she finished he shook his head slowly. "The quizlet has it. Look." He held out his phone, and she read the screen twice, then a third time, because the sentence refused to fit into her drawing. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP. The fuel didn't enter the power plant first. It was broken in half on the doorstep, in the open soup of the cell, and only the pieces went inside.

"Outside," she said. "The first step is outside." She crossed out her arrow with the marker until the rock went gray, then drew a new one that stopped short of the bean, in the empty space she had thought of as nothing. That nothing was the cytoplasm. That nothing was where everything started. "One glucose in, two pyruvate out," she said, sketching the two smaller shapes like a split river around a stone, "and you get two ATP for it. Net. Only two, even though it feels like it should be more." Theo nodded and folded the phone away.

He watched her redraw the whole diagram from memory, and from where he stood the marker looked like a small walking stick in her fist. She had always wanted certainty from him, wanted him to contextualize each fact inside some larger order so that memorizing felt like discovering rather than copying, and he had never been able to give her that, because the order kept revising itself in his own lectures and textbooks. But she was building one anyway, arrow by arrow, in ink that a rainstorm could wash off the rock by morning. He thought of the tutoring flyer in the student center, the neat promises of guaranteed results, and of how false their verisimilitude was, how polished and how empty. His sister's lopsided circle, wrong arrow and all, was more honest than any flyer.

"The rest goes in the mitochondria, then," she said. "The pyruvate goes in and the real ATP gets made there. So the cell gets two quick coins outside and then the whole paycheck inside." She looked up. "Is that right?" Theo opened his mouth and closed it. "Mostly," he said. "Ask me again at the top of the trail." She capped the marker, put the notebook under her arm, and started up the switchbacks ahead of him, reciting under her breath, "Cytoplasm, cytoplasm, cytoplasm," like a word she was teaching her feet.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph.
story:
The speedometer needle trembled between thirty and thirty-two, and Alexis wrote "32" in the margin of her chemistry notebook, next to the clock on the dashboard that read 4:07. Her grandmother drove the long way home from Dr. Patel's office because the highway scared her now, and Alexis had promised, two weeks ago, not to comment on the route. So she commented on the speed instead, silently, every minute, in a column that was growing down the page like a tapeworm. 4:08, 28. 4:09, 25. The car slowed for the light at Marsh Road, and the needle sagged to zero, and Alexis wrote that too, feeling faintly ridiculous, feeling like a scientist.

The ridiculousness was the point. On Thursday, Mr. Okafor had assigned them an integral for homework, a genuine area-under-a-curve problem, and Alexis had stared at it the way you stare at a word you've written so many times it stops looking like a word. She knew the procedure. She could execute the procedure in her sleep. What she could not see was what the procedure was for, and this bothered her more than getting it wrong would have, because a wrong answer could be checked. A meaningless right answer just sat there.

At the following math club meeting, the room smelled like the burnt coffee Marcus always made in the teacher's lounge without permission, and Marcus was already excoriating the freshmen for their bracket predictions, though basketball had nothing to do with anything, and everyone knew the excoriation was a performance he ran to hide the fact that he wanted, badly, to be chosen for the regional team and had not yet been. "You're going to exhaust yourself," Alexis told him, and he said, "I am already exhausted, it's very glamorous," and poured her a cup without being asked, which was the kind of thing Marcus did.

She spread her notebook on the table between them. "I need you to look at this and tell me if I've lost my mind." The column of numbers ran down the margin, each with its timestamp. "My grandmother drove me home Tuesday. I read the speedometer every minute. That's the speed, right? Miles per hour, one reading per minute."

Marcus leaned over it with the sardonic expression he wore when he was actually interested, which Alexis had learned to read as encouragement. "You timed your grandmother."

"I timed my grandmother. Now here's my question." She drew the axes on a fresh sheet of paper, time along the bottom, speed up the side, and began plotting her points, connecting them with short line segments so the graph rose and fell like a shallow saw. "If I want to know how far we went, the distance we traveled in the car, is this it? Is this the thing?" She tapped the ragged shape under the line. "The area under this curve is the distance. The integral of the speed over the time we drove."

"You're asking me," Marcus said, "whether the area under a velocity graph is displacement."

"Is that the word?"

"That's the word. Integrating a velocity function over a time interval gives you the displacement, which is the area under the velocity-time graph. It's like the first thing they put in every textbook, and it's why anyone cared about any of this in the first place." He said it lightly, not lecturing, more like someone confirming a rumor. Then he went still over her page. "Wait. You have actual data."

She had actual data. They spent the next forty minutes on it while the freshmen argued about brackets behind them and the coffee went cold. Her readings were one minute apart, so each one was a skinny rectangle, one minute wide and whatever speed she'd recorded high, and when she added all the rectangles up, adjusting for the ones where the needle had moved between readings, she got a number: a little over nine miles. She sat back. Nine miles was nothing. Nine miles was the distance to the dentist.

Here was what she could not decide, and she said so out loud, because the whole point of math club, as far as Alexis was concerned, was that you could say the uncertain part out loud. "I know the area under the curve is the distance. I believe that now, I've seen it work. But my graph isn't the real velocity. It's a staircase. The car didn't move in staircases. So my answer is close and it's also wrong, and I can't tell how wrong, and I don't know whether to be happy about it or not."

Marcus, who wanted certainty the way other people wanted sleep, frowned at her rectangles as if they'd personally deceived him. "Take more readings. Every thirty seconds. Every ten."

"Then every five, then every one, and I still never get there."

"Right," he said slowly. "But you get closer." He picked up her pen and drew her a little diagonal slash cutting the corner off one of her staircase steps, where her graph said 32 and then 28 and the truth had presumably been somewhere in between. "That little triangle. That's your error. It shrinks." He looked almost betrayed by this, because a lemma he loved, the tidy one about error bounds, was now implicated in her grandmother's driving, and nothing in the textbook had prepared him for that.

After the meeting, Alexis walked to the parking lot and sat on the concrete wall by the flagpole and called her grandmother, who answered on the fourth ring the way she always did, as if the phone were a small animal she had to approach calmly. "Grandma. Tuesday, when you drove me home. Did we go about nine miles?" There was a pause, and the sound of the kitchen radio, and then her grandmother said, "Nine and a half, I'd say, I looked at the odometer," and Alexis looked down at her notebook, at the ragged sawtooth curve with its crooked staircase underneath, and laughed once, quietly, into the phone.

"Grandma, next time you drive me somewhere, can you take the long way again?"
